name: Classic-Style Test 5
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Media critic: The Regional Press Council has urged newspapers to stop printing photographs of accident victims without the consent of the victims' families. But several of the council's own members are editors whose papers have printed such photographs in the past. So the council's recommendation does not deserve to be taken seriously.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the media critic's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes that a recommendation followed by most newspapers must be a sound one
rejects a recommendation on the grounds that some of those who make it have not acted in accordance with it
fails to consider that printing photographs of accident victims might sometimes serve the public interest
draws a conclusion about all newspapers from the past conduct of only a few editors
confuses the council's authority to recommend a practice with its authority to enforce that practice
questions.explanation: Whether a recommendation is sound has nothing to do with whether the people making it have always followed it; (B) names this tu quoque flaw. (C) is tempting because it raises a point about the merits, but the critic never addresses the merits at all, and considering that point would only help the critic's conclusion. (D) fails because the critic draws no conclusion about all newspapers.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The council's recommendation against printing accident-victim photos without family consent shouldn't be taken seriously.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some council members edit papers that have printed such photos.

breakdown.analysis: So what if some council members didn't practice what they preach? A recommendation is good or bad on its merits, not on the track record of the people making it. This is the tu quoque flaw, a kind of ad hominem: 'you do it too, so your advice is worthless.' It's a classic; know it. It's like ignoring your doctor's advice to quit smoking because your doctor smokes. We need an answer that says the critic dismisses advice because its givers don't follow it.

choices.note: The critic never says the recommendation is popular or that most papers follow it. Wrong flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Nearly every newspaper in the region already follows the council's guideline, so the guideline must be a wise one.

choices.note: CORRECT. That's exactly the move: the editors' own past conduct is used to dismiss what the council recommends. Hypocrisy in the messengers doesn't make the message wrong.

Tempting, because it sounds like a fair point about the merits. But the critic never touches the merits, and this point would only support the critic's side. Failing to consider a point that helps you isn't the flaw here.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Printing such photos causes families pain, so it is never justified (ignoring that a photo might reveal a dangerous road design).

choices.note: The conclusion is about the council's recommendation, not about all newspapers. No generalization happens.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Three editors I know printed such photos, so every newspaper in the country does it.

choices.note: Enforcement never comes up. The critic doesn't argue that the council can't enforce its advice.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The council can't punish papers that ignore its guideline, so the guideline must be mistaken.

questions.stimulus: Forester: Many landowners in the Brenna Hills believe that clearing all the dead wood from their woodlots makes the woods healthier. This belief is mistaken. Fallen logs shelter the salamanders and ground beetles that keep pest insects in check, and as the logs rot they return nutrients to the soil. Removing them, then, deprives the remaining trees of both protection and nourishment.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the forester's argument?
choices: Fallen logs shelter animals that keep pest insects in check.
Landowners in the Brenna Hills should leave all the dead wood in their woodlots.
Removing fallen logs deprives the remaining trees of both protection and nourishment.
Clearing all the dead wood from a woodlot does not make the woods healthier.
Rotting logs return more nutrients to the soil than any other source does.
questions.explanation: The forester's point is that the landowners' belief is mistaken, which (D) restates: clearing all the dead wood doesn't make the woods healthier. (C) is tempting because it follows 'then,' but it is an intermediate conclusion that supports the rejection of the belief. (B) adds a recommendation the forester never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The belief that clearing all dead wood makes woods healthier is mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. Fallen logs shelter pest-eating salamanders and beetles; 2. rotting logs feed the soil; 3. so removing them costs trees protection and nourishment.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. 'This belief is mistaken' is the main point; the facts about logs explain why, and the 'then' sentence pulls those facts together into a sub-conclusion that in turn supports 'mistaken.' Watch out: the last sentence has a conclusion word, but it's a stepping stone. We need an answer that restates 'the belief is wrong.'

choices.note: This is a premise, one of the reasons the belief is wrong. Premises are never the main conclusion.
Too strong, and it adds a recommendation. The forester says clearing everything doesn't help; that's not the same as telling landowners to leave every scrap of dead wood.

Tempting, because of the word 'then.' But this sentence is an intermediate conclusion: it's the reason the forester gives for calling the belief mistaken. It supports the main point rather than being it.
CORRECT. 'This belief is mistaken' just means it's false that clearing all the dead wood makes woods healthier. Everything else in the stimulus supports this.
Unsupported superlative. The forester says rotting logs return nutrients, not that they're the biggest source.

questions.stimulus: Immunologist: In a study of 400 adults, those who slept at least seven hours a night during the week after receiving a hepatitis vaccine produced substantially more antibodies against the virus than did those who slept less. Thus, getting adequate sleep after vaccination enhances the body's antibody response to the vaccine.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the immunologist's argument?
choices: The participants who slept less were, on average, no older and no less healthy than the others, and age and health both affect antibody production.
Some participants who slept more than nine hours a night produced fewer antibodies than some who slept exactly seven hours.
The antibodies produced in response to the hepatitis vaccine decline gradually over a period of several years.
Most adults report sleeping fewer than seven hours on at least some nights each week.
Producing antibodies is only one of several ways in which the immune system responds to a vaccine.
questions.explanation: The study shows only a correlation between sleep and antibody levels; older or less healthy people might both sleep less and respond more weakly. (A) rules out those alternative causes, so the sleep difference becomes the more likely explanation. (B) is tempting but compares people within the well-rested group and, if anything, muddies the link.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Adequate sleep after vaccination boosts the antibody response.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a study, people who slept 7+ hours in the week after the vaccine made more antibodies than people who slept less.

breakdown.analysis: Is it the sleep, or something about the people who sleep less? Older people and sicker people often sleep worse, and they might make fewer antibodies regardless. That's a correlation dressed up as a cause. We need an answer that rules out a different difference between the two groups.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the short sleepers weren't older or sicker, two obvious alternative explanations are gone. That makes sleep itself the more likely cause.

Tempting, because it's about sleep and antibodies. But it compares people inside the well-rested group, and 'some' vs. 'some' tells us almost nothing. If anything it slightly weakens a simple more-sleep-is-better story.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. How long antibodies last says nothing about whether sleep boosted how many were made.
So? How common short sleep is doesn't bear on whether sleep causes a better response.
Irrelevant. The conclusion is only about the antibody response, so other immune responses don't matter.

questions.stimulus: For the past four months the volcano Mount Teral has been erupting mildly, and fine ash has fallen almost daily on the nearby village of Ostin. Yet the number of patients seeking treatment for breathing problems at Ostin's only clinic has fallen sharply since the eruptions began.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Volcanic ash can irritate the lungs even of people who have no history of breathing problems.
Ostin's clinic is the only medical facility within a day's travel of the village.
Since the eruptions began, most of Ostin's residents have been staying with relatives in towns outside the area where ash is falling.
The ash falling on Ostin consists of particles small enough to remain in the air for several hours.
Several larger towns farther from Mount Teral have also received light falls of ash.
questions.explanation: If most residents have left the ash zone, there are far fewer people around to seek treatment at the clinic, so the number of patients can fall even though the ash is harmful. (A) and (D) only deepen the puzzle by making the ash sound worse, and (B) suggests everyone with breathing trouble would still go to that clinic.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Ash has been falling on Ostin daily, but fewer people are visiting the clinic for breathing problems.

breakdown.analysis: How can breathing complaints drop when the air is full of ash? Notice the stimulus counts patients, not the rate among residents. If the people aren't there, they can't show up at the clinic. We need an answer that explains why fewer patients would come in despite the ash.

choices.note: This makes the ash sound more dangerous, so we'd expect more patients. It deepens the paradox.
This makes it even stranger: if it's the only facility nearby, anyone with breathing trouble should be showing up there.
CORRECT. Most residents are gone. Fewer people in the village means fewer patients at the clinic, even if the ash is bad for the people who stayed.
Again, this makes the ash more harmful, since it stays in the air longer. It deepens the puzzle.
Right topic, wrong place. Other towns' ash doesn't explain what's happening at Ostin's clinic.

questions.stimulus: Music educator: Our district wants more high school students to join the orchestra. Most students who join the high school orchestra took string lessons in the district's elementary schools, but the district eliminated those lessons last year. So unless the elementary string lessons are restored, membership in the high school orchestra will decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the music educator's argument?
choices: Students who took elementary string lessons play more skillfully in high school than students who did not.
Most students who took elementary string lessons in the district went on to join the high school orchestra.
Restoring the elementary string lessons would cost the district less than recruiting orchestra members in other ways.
No student who did not take elementary string lessons has ever joined the high school orchestra.
Not all of the students who would have taken the elementary string lessons will instead take private string lessons outside school.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes that losing the school lessons means losing the training that feeds the orchestra; if every would-be student simply took private lessons instead, the pipeline would be unaffected. (E) states the modest assumption that not all of them will. (B) is tempting but reverses the premise: the argument says most joiners had lessons, not that most lesson-takers joined, and it doesn't need the latter.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Unless elementary string lessons come back, high school orchestra membership will fall.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most orchestra members took the elementary lessons; the district cut those lessons last year.

breakdown.analysis: Does cutting the school lessons actually mean kids won't learn strings? What if every one of them just signs up for private lessons? Then the orchestra still gets trained players and nothing changes. We need an answer that blocks the 'they'll learn elsewhere' escape. Test by negation.

choices.note: Skill isn't the issue; the argument is about how many students join. Negate it and the membership argument is untouched.
choices.negation: Students who took elementary string lessons do not play more skillfully in high school than students who did not.

choices.note: Tempting, but it flips the premise. The educator says most joiners had lessons, not that most lesson-takers joined. Negate it: maybe only 30% of lesson-takers joined. Losing the lessons could still shrink the orchestra.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most students who took elementary string lessons went on to join the orchestra.

choices.note: Wrong dimension: cost. The argument predicts a decline; it doesn't compare the price of different fixes. Negation does nothing.
choices.negation: Restoring the lessons would not cost less than recruiting members in other ways.

choices.note: Too strong. The premise says 'most,' so some members might have skipped the lessons. Negate it and the argument is fine.
choices.negation: At least one student who did not take elementary string lessons has joined the high school orchestra.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: all of the students who would have taken the lessons will take private lessons instead. Then the pipeline is intact and there's no reason to expect a decline. The argument falls apart.
choices.negation: All of the students who would have taken the elementary string lessons will instead take private string lessons outside school.

questions.stimulus: Ralston Hardware sells two brands of interior paint, Corvo and Tenly, at the same price per gallon. A gallon of Corvo covers about 400 square feet of wall with one coat, whereas a gallon of Tenly covers about 300 square feet. In independent tests, a single coat of either brand fully hid the old color on most walls.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Covering a given area of wall with one coat will generally cost a Ralston customer less with Corvo than with Tenly.
Corvo is a higher-quality paint than Tenly in most of the respects that matter to customers.
Ralston sells more gallons of Corvo than of Tenly in a typical year.
Tenly costs its maker more per gallon to manufacture than Corvo does.
Two coats of Tenly hide old colors better than one coat of Corvo does.
questions.explanation: Same price per gallon, but Corvo covers a third more area per gallon, and one coat of either usually suffices, so covering a given area takes less Corvo and therefore less money (A). (B) stretches 'covers more area' into overall quality, and (C) and (D) introduce sales and manufacturing costs the facts never mention.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Corvo and Tenly cost the same per gallon; 2. a gallon of Corvo covers ~400 sq ft, Tenly ~300; 3. one coat of either usually hides the old color.

breakdown.analysis: Put facts 1 and 2 together: same price, but Corvo stretches farther. Fact 3 says one coat of either usually does the job, so you don't need extra Corvo to make up for weaker coverage. That means the same wall costs less with Corvo. We need an answer about cost per area.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same price per gallon, more square feet per gallon, and one coat usually suffices. So a given area needs fewer gallons of Corvo, and fewer gallons at the same price means less money.
Tempting, because Corvo goes farther. But 'covers more area' isn't 'higher quality.' Quality could include durability, color, smell. We only know about coverage.
We know nothing about sales. Customers might prefer Tenly for any number of reasons.
Manufacturing cost never comes up. Same shelf price tells us nothing about production cost.
The facts never compare two coats of one brand with one coat of the other. Unsupported.

questions.stimulus: Botanist: The Vessian oak grows an unusually thick, spongy bark. The tree is native to hillsides where wildfires sweep through every few decades, and thick bark insulates a tree's living tissue from heat. So the Vessian oak's bark is probably an adaptation that protects the tree from fire.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the botanist's argument?
choices: Most wildfires in the Vessian oak's native range burn through the undergrowth on the hillsides without ever reaching the treetops.
Vessian oaks whose bark has been stripped by people are more likely than other Vessian oaks to die in wildfires.
The Vessian oak's spongy bark absorbs rainwater in the wet season and supplies it to the tree during the long summer droughts.
Some tree species that are not native to fire-prone regions also have bark that insulates them from heat.
Growing thick bark requires a tree to use resources that it could otherwise devote to growing taller.
questions.explanation: The botanist infers a trait's function from the fact that it would help with fire. (C) offers a different job the spongy bark does, storing water for droughts, which gives another explanation for why the trait evolved. (B) is tempting but strengthens the argument by showing that bark does protect against fire.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Vessian oak's thick, spongy bark is probably an adaptation for fire protection.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The oak lives where wildfires happen; thick bark insulates against heat.

breakdown.analysis: Just because a trait could help with fire, does that mean that's what it's for? Lots of traits fit more than one story. This is a function guess, and the standard way to weaken one is to give the trait a different job. It's like deciding a dog's thick coat is for protection from thorns when it's really for warmth. We need an answer that offers another explanation for spongy bark.

choices.note: This doesn't touch the bark. If anything, ground fires reaching the trunk would make thick bark more useful, so it leans toward the botanist.
Tempting, because it's about bark and fire. But it shows bark does protect against fire, so it strengthens. Wrong direction.

CORRECT. Now there's a second job for the bark: the 'spongy' part stores water for droughts. That gives a strong alternative explanation for why the oak evolved this trait, so the fire story is less likely to be the reason.
Wrong group. Other species' bark doesn't tell us why the Vessian oak's bark evolved. Insulating bark existing elsewhere is consistent with the botanist's view.
So? Every trait has costs. A cost doesn't say what the benefit is for, and it fits a fire story just as well.

questions.stimulus:
Ortega: The city should rezone the old rail yard on Fulton Street to allow housing. The neighborhood badly needs new homes, and the yard has sat empty for twenty years.

Kim: The neighborhood certainly needs homes. But the rail yard's soil is soaked with diesel residue, and cleaning it up would cost more than any developer could recover by selling homes there. Rezoning the yard for housing would accomplish nothing; it should remain zoned for industry.
questions.stem: Ortega and Kim disagree over whether
choices: the neighborhood around Fulton Street needs more housing
the Fulton Street rail yard should be rezoned to allow housing
the soil at the Fulton Street rail yard is contaminated
the rail yard has been empty for twenty years
developers should be required to pay for cleaning up contaminated sites
questions.explanation: Ortega says the yard should be rezoned for housing; Kim says it should stay zoned for industry, so they disagree about (B). (A) is something both affirm, since Kim concedes the neighborhood needs homes. Ortega says nothing about the soil (C), and Kim says nothing about how long the yard has been empty (D).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ortega: rezone the yard for housing, since homes are needed and the site is empty; Kim: homes are needed, but cleanup costs make housing there pointless, so keep it industrial.

breakdown.analysis: Where do they actually clash? Kim agrees homes are needed, so that's common ground. The clash is the proposal itself: Ortega says rezone, Kim says don't. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. We need the answer that both speakers take a side on, and opposite sides.

choices.note: Tempting because it's Ortega's main reason. But Kim explicitly agrees ('certainly needs homes'). That's agreement, not disagreement.
CORRECT. Ortega: yes, rezone. Kim: no, keep it industrial. Clear yes vs. no.
Only Kim talks about the soil. Ortega never says whether it's contaminated, so we can't call it a disagreement.
Only Ortega mentions this, and Kim never disputes it.
Neither speaker says who should pay for cleanup. Kim just says it would cost more than a developer could recover.

questions.stimulus: Safety inspector: A warehouse robot may be certified to work alongside people only if it passes the Callan collision test. The Model K7 robot detects obstacles solely with cameras; it has no laser rangefinder. So the K7 cannot be certified to work alongside people.
questions.stem: The safety inspector's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any robot that is equipped with a laser rangefinder can pass the Callan collision test.
Most robots that detect obstacles solely with cameras fail the Callan collision test.
Robots that pass the Callan collision test rarely collide with people.
No robot that lacks a laser rangefinder can pass the Callan collision test.
A robot that cannot be certified to work alongside people should not be sold to warehouses.
questions.explanation: Certified requires passing the Callan test, so we need a link showing the K7 can't pass; (D) says passing requires a rangefinder, which the K7 lacks. (A) is the tempting reversal: it says a rangefinder is enough to pass, which tells us nothing about robots without one. (B) says 'most,' leaving room for the K7 to pass.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The K7 can't be certified to work alongside people.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Certified → passes Callan test; the K7 has no laser rangefinder.

breakdown.analysis: What does a rangefinder have to do with the Callan test? Nothing, so far. The chain is: Certified → Passes Callan. To show the K7 isn't certified, we need it to fail the test. Contrapositive: not Passes → not Certified. So we need: no rangefinder → can't pass, which is the same as Passes → has rangefinder. Then: K7 has no rangefinder → can't pass → can't be certified. We need the rangefinder to be a necessary condition for passing, not a sufficient one.

choices.note: Tempting, because it links the rangefinder to the test. But it's backwards: Rangefinder → Passes. That says nothing about robots without one. The K7 might pass some other way.
'Most' isn't 'all.' The K7 could be in the minority that passes, so the conclusion doesn't follow.
Irrelevant. How well passing robots perform afterward doesn't tell us whether the K7 can pass.
CORRECT. Passes → Rangefinder. The K7 has no rangefinder, so it can't pass, so it can't be certified. The chain is complete.
This adds a consequence (not selling to warehouses) after the conclusion. It doesn't help get to the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Store manager: Last year, 20 percent of the items our customers ordered online were returned, compared with only 5 percent of the items bought in our stores. Clearly, then, our returns staff spent more of their time last year processing returns of online orders than processing returns of in-store purchases.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the store manager's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes that customers who return items are dissatisfied with the store
fails to consider that some customers shop both online and in the store
takes for granted that returned items cannot be sold again
draws a conclusion about all retailers from data about a single store
overlooks the possibility that far fewer items were ordered online than were bought in the stores
questions.explanation: A higher return rate doesn't mean more returns: if in-store sales vastly outnumber online orders, 5 percent of a large number can exceed 20 percent of a small one, and the staff's time tracks the number of returns. (E) points this out. (B) is tempting but irrelevant, since a customer's shopping both ways doesn't change how many returns of each kind there were.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Returns staff spent more time on online returns than on in-store returns.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 20% of online items were returned vs. 5% of in-store items.

breakdown.analysis: Does a higher percentage mean a bigger pile of returns? Not if the bases differ. Imagine 1,000 online items (200 returns) and 10,000 in-store items (500 returns). The online rate is four times higher, but the staff handled more in-store returns. Watch the switch from a rate to an absolute amount; it's a classic, know it. We need an answer that says the manager ignored how many items each channel sold.

choices.note: Customer satisfaction never comes up. The argument is about staff time.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Twice as many online items were returned, so our online customers must dislike us.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a complication. But it doesn't matter who made the purchases; what matters is how many returns of each type there were.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Online shoppers return more items, so the people who shop online must be pickier (ignoring that the same people also shop in the store).

choices.note: The manager never assumes anything about reselling. Irrelevant to staff time.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Returns cost us money, since every returned item has to be thrown away.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about this store's staff. No generalization to other retailers.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our online return rate is high, so online shopping causes high return rates everywhere.

choices.note: CORRECT. Rates don't tell you totals. If in-store sales were much larger, 5% of them could be more returns than 20% of the online orders, and then the staff would spend more time on in-store returns.

questions.stimulus: Zoning principle: A variance allowing a new building to exceed the local height limit should be granted whenever the added height will not cast a shadow on any public park and the developer either includes affordable housing units in the building or restores a historic facade on the site.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: The Rowan Street tower will include affordable units and restore a historic facade, though its added height will shade a corner of Rowan Park in the late afternoon. So its variance should be granted.
The Delmar office building's added height will not shade any park, but it will include no affordable units and restore no historic facade. So its variance should be denied.

The Parkway hotel's added height will not shade any park, and its developer will restore the 1890s bank facade on the site, though the hotel will include no housing. So its variance should be granted.
The Linden apartment building will include affordable units, and its developer says the shade its added height casts on Linden Park will be minor. So its variance should be granted.
The Corso building's added height will not shade any park, and its developer has promised to consider including affordable units. So its variance should be granted.
questions.explanation: The principle requires no shadow on any park plus either affordable units or a restored historic facade; the Parkway hotel meets the shadow condition and the facade half of the 'or,' so (C) conforms. (B) is tempting, but the principle states only when a variance should be granted, so it can never by itself justify a denial. (A) and (D) involve shade on a park, and (E) offers only a promise to consider affordable units.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: No shadow on any public park AND (affordable units OR restored historic facade) → grant the variance.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The right answer must grant a variance where 1. the added height shades no park and 2. the developer does at least one of: includes affordable units, restores a historic facade.

breakdown.analysis: What does the principle let you conclude? Only 'grant.' It never says when to deny, so any 'deny' answer is out. For 'grant,' check two things: no park shade at all, and at least one half of the 'or.' Each trap satisfies only part.

choices.note: Both halves of the 'or' are met, but the shadow condition fails: it shades a corner of Rowan Park. 'Any public park' means even a corner counts.

Tempting, because this building does fail the 'or.' But the principle only tells you when to grant. Failing its conditions doesn't trigger a denial; the principle is silent. This confuses a sufficient condition with a necessary one.
CORRECT. No park shade, and the developer restores a historic facade, which satisfies the 'or' by itself. The missing housing doesn't matter. Grant follows.
Affordable units satisfy the 'or,' but the building does shade Linden Park. 'Minor' shade is still shade, and the developer's say-so doesn't change that.
No shade, but a promise to consider affordable units isn't including them, and there's no facade. The 'or' isn't satisfied.

questions.stimulus: When the Harwick supermarket chain cut the price of its own-brand olive oil by 25 percent last spring, it expected sales of the oil to rise. Instead, sales fell, even though the prices of competing brands at Harwick stores did not change and the oil itself was not altered in any way.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why sales of Harwick's own-brand olive oil fell?
choices: Many shoppers who buy olive oil judge its quality largely by its price.
Before the price cut, Harwick's own-brand olive oil was already the least expensive olive oil sold in its stores.
Olive oil sales at other supermarket chains rose last spring.
Harwick advertised the price cut prominently in its weekly flyers.
The price that Harwick paid its suppliers for olive oil rose sharply last year.
questions.explanation: If shoppers read a low price as a sign of low quality, a deep price cut could make the oil look inferior and drive buyers to other brands, explaining the drop (A). (B) is tempting, but already being the cheapest gives no reason why becoming even cheaper would lose sales. (D) deepens the puzzle, since advertising should have helped.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Harwick cut its own-brand olive oil price by 25%, but sales fell, with competitors' prices and the oil itself unchanged.

breakdown.analysis: Why would a cheaper product sell less? The stimulus rules out the easy answers: competitors didn't cut prices, and the oil didn't change. So the explanation must be about how shoppers react to the price itself. Common sense helps: lots of people assume cheap means worse. We need an answer that makes a lower price a reason to buy less.

choices.note: CORRECT. If shoppers use price as a quality signal, a 25% cut makes the oil look worse, so some switch to pricier brands. That explains falling sales without contradicting anything.
Tempting, because it seems to matter that it was already cheapest. But it doesn't explain why getting even cheaper would cost sales. It leaves the puzzle in place.
This makes it stranger: oil was selling well elsewhere, so the fall at Harwick isn't a general market slump.
This deepens the puzzle. More shoppers knew about the lower price, so sales should have risen.
Wrong dimension: Harwick's costs. What Harwick paid suppliers doesn't explain why shoppers bought less.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: Varga defines a robot as any machine that senses its surroundings and acts on what it senses without moment-to-moment human direction. But an ordinary household thermostat senses the temperature of a room and switches the furnace on or off with no one directing it. And no one would call a thermostat a robot.
questions.stem: The philosopher's argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that a proposed definition is too narrow because it excludes some machines that are clearly robots
questioning whether Varga has the expertise needed to define a technical term
proposing a more precise definition that avoids the difficulty the argument identifies
appealing to the authority of the engineers who design and build robots
describing a case that meets the conditions of a proposed definition but does not belong to the category being defined
questions.explanation: The thermostat satisfies Varga's conditions (it senses and acts without human direction) yet isn't a robot, showing the definition is too broad; (E) describes this. (A) is the tempting reversal: the philosopher shows the definition lets in too much, not that it leaves out real robots. (C) fails because no alternative definition is offered.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Implicit) Varga's definition of 'robot' is flawed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A thermostat senses and acts without human direction, so it fits the definition; but nobody calls a thermostat a robot.

breakdown.analysis: Is the thermostat a robot that the definition leaves out, or a non-robot the definition lets in? It's a non-robot that gets in. That's a counterexample showing the definition is too broad. A definition can fail two ways: too broad (includes things it shouldn't) or too narrow (excludes things it should). We need an answer that describes a case fitting the definition but not the category.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the right method (a counterexample to a definition) with the direction reversed. A thermostat isn't a robot being shut out; it's a non-robot being let in. That's too broad, not too narrow.
choices.example: Example of this method: Varga says robots must have arms. But a self-driving delivery cart has no arms, and it's clearly a robot.

choices.note: The philosopher never mentions Varga's qualifications. No attack on the person.
choices.example: Example of this method: Varga is a philosopher, not an engineer, so why should we accept her definition of a robot?

choices.note: No new definition appears. The philosopher only shows the old one fails.
choices.example: Example of this method: Varga's definition includes thermostats, so let's define a robot as a machine that senses, acts, and can change its own goals.

choices.note: The appeal is to ordinary usage ('no one would call'), not to engineers or any experts.
choices.example: Example of this method: Robotics engineers don't consider thermostats robots, so Varga's definition is wrong.

choices.note: CORRECT. The thermostat meets both of Varga's conditions, sensing and acting without moment-to-moment direction, yet it isn't a robot. That's a counterexample showing the definition is too broad.

questions.stimulus: Consumer reporter: Each year our magazine prices the same basket of groceries at the twelve largest supermarkets in the county. Two years ago, Valdane Foods had the cheapest basket of the twelve; this year it ranked only fifth. So shoppers who have stayed loyal to Valdane are now paying more for their groceries than they were two years ago.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the consumer reporter's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes that Valdane's loyal shoppers choose where to shop solely on the basis of price
overlooks the possibility that Valdane fell in the rankings because other supermarkets lowered their prices, not because Valdane raised its own
takes for granted that the magazine priced the basket of groceries in the same way in both years
draws a conclusion about all twelve supermarkets from information about only one of them
fails to consider that shoppers who stopped going to Valdane may now be paying more at other supermarkets
questions.explanation: A ranking is relative: Valdane can drop from first to fifth while its own prices stay flat or even fall, if four rivals cut prices more. (B) points out that the argument treats a drop in rank as an absolute price increase. (C) is tempting but merely possible, and since the rankings compare stores within each year, a change in method wouldn't by itself rescue the leap from rank to price.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Loyal Valdane shoppers pay more for groceries now than two years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Valdane went from cheapest of twelve to fifth cheapest in the magazine's basket comparison.

breakdown.analysis: Does falling in a ranking mean your number went up? No. Rankings are relative. If you run the same time in a race but four people speed up, you drop to fifth without getting any slower. Valdane might even have cut prices, just by less than its rivals. This is the ranking-to-absolute shift; watch for it whenever a conclusion about 'more' or 'less' comes from a rank. We need an answer that says other stores' changes could explain the drop.

choices.note: The argument isn't about why shoppers pick stores; it's about what loyal shoppers pay. Nothing here assumes price is their only reason.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Valdane is no longer the cheapest, so its loyal shoppers will surely leave for a cheaper store.

choices.note: CORRECT. Fifth place only tells you four stores are now cheaper. That can happen with Valdane's prices unchanged or lower, so the drop in rank doesn't show its shoppers pay more.

Tempting, because a change in method sounds like a real worry. But nothing suggests the method changed, and even with an identical method, a drop in rank wouldn't show that Valdane's prices rose. It's merely possible and doesn't hit the gap.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our survey found Valdane cheapest two years ago and fifth this year, so prices there must have risen (when this year's survey used a different basket).

choices.note: The conclusion is about Valdane's shoppers only. No claim about all twelve stores.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Valdane's prices went up, so prices at all twelve supermarkets must have gone up.

choices.note: Wrong group. The conclusion is about shoppers who stayed loyal, not those who left.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Former Valdane shoppers pay more now, so loyal Valdane shoppers must pay more too.

questions.stimulus: Every reporter at the Daily Ledger was asked in an anonymous survey how thoroughly he or she checks facts before submitting a story. Most of the reporters said that they check facts more thoroughly than most of the paper's other reporters do.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most of the Ledger's reporters overestimate how thoroughly they check facts compared with their colleagues.
The Ledger's reporters check facts less thoroughly than do reporters at most other newspapers.
The wording of the survey encouraged the Ledger's reporters to rate themselves favorably.
Some of the Ledger's reporters are mistaken, or untruthful, about how thoroughly they check facts relative to the paper's other reporters.
Reporters who check facts thoroughly are less likely than others to have to print corrections.
questions.explanation: Fewer than half of a group can each be more thorough than most of the others, so if most claim it, at least some of those claims are wrong (D). (A) is the tempting overreach: the facts guarantee only that some are wrong; if six of ten reporters make the claim and the top five make it truthfully, just one is mistaken. (C) is merely possible.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. All Ledger reporters were surveyed; 2. most said they check facts more thoroughly than most of the paper's other reporters.

breakdown.analysis: Can most people be better than most others? No. Picture 10 reporters ranked by thoroughness. To beat most of the other 9, you need to beat at least 5 of them, which only the top 5 can do. So if 6 or more say they're in that group, at least one is wrong (or fibbing). But notice how little that guarantees: 'some' are wrong, not 'most.' Watch for answers that inflate 'some' to 'most.'

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the punch line. But too strong. If 6 of 10 claim it and the top 5 are telling the truth, only 1 is wrong, which is nowhere near most of the reporters.
Other newspapers never appear. The survey only compares Ledger reporters with each other.
Merely possible. Nothing in the facts tells us how the survey was worded, and the inference works with any wording.

CORRECT. The math forces it: not everyone who claims to be above most colleagues can be. So at least some reporters are wrong or not telling the truth. 'Mistaken, or untruthful' covers both ways that can happen.
Corrections never come up. This adds a new claim about consequences of fact-checking.

questions.stimulus: Volcanologist: Over the past three months, the ground on the northern flank of Mount Karsa has risen by four centimeters. Ground can swell when heavy rains saturate the rock beneath it, but it also rises when magma accumulates below the surface. So magma is probably accumulating beneath Karsa's northern flank.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the volcanologist's argument?
choices: Mount Karsa has erupted several times over the past two centuries.
Ground that rises because of accumulating magma often continues rising for months before an eruption begins.
Rainfall in the region around Mount Karsa over the past three months has been the lowest recorded in decades.
In past decades, the ground on Karsa's northern flank has risen and fallen several times without any eruption following.
Magma that accumulates beneath a volcano does not always lead to an eruption.
questions.explanation: The volcanologist names two possible causes of swelling, heavy rain and magma, and picks magma; (C) rules out the rain explanation, leaving magma as the likely cause. (B) is tempting but describes what magma-driven swelling does without showing that this swelling is magma-driven.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Magma is probably accumulating under Karsa's northern flank.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The flank rose 4 cm in three months; swelling can come from heavy rain or from magma.

breakdown.analysis: The stimulus hands you the alternative: rain. So why pick magma? Nothing in the argument rules out rain. Strengthening here is easy once you see it: take the other suspect off the table. We need an answer that says it wasn't rain.

choices.note: Background. A history of eruptions doesn't tell us whether this particular swelling comes from magma or rain.
Tempting, because it connects swelling and magma. But it describes magma swelling; it doesn't show that this swelling is magma swelling. Rain is still on the table.
CORRECT. If it's been an exceptionally dry three months, the rain explanation is out. That leaves magma as the best explanation for the rise.
If anything this slightly weakens: the flank rises and falls often, so this rise may be nothing special. It certainly doesn't help.
Irrelevant. The conclusion is about magma accumulating, not about whether an eruption will follow.

questions.stimulus: Council member: Three years ago, the city rezoned the Harbor Street corridor to forbid any new building taller than four stories. Not a single new office building has been built along the corridor since then. Clearly, the rezoning has discouraged office development there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the council member's argument depends?
choices: Had the corridor not been rezoned, at least one new office building would likely have been built along it during the past three years.
Most developers who build office buildings prefer to build ones that are taller than four stories.
No new residential buildings have been built along the Harbor Street corridor since the rezoning either.
Before the rezoning, at least one office building taller than four stories had been built along the corridor.
Demand for office space in the city has not declined at all over the past three years.
questions.explanation: Blaming the rezoning for the lack of office construction assumes that, without the rezoning, some office building would likely have gone up; if none would have been built anyway, the evidence shows nothing about the rezoning's effect (A). (E) is the attractive trap: a modest decline in demand is compatible with the argument, so the assumption is far stronger than required. (B) is also too strong, since even a minority of developers wanting taller buildings could be discouraged.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The rezoning discouraged office development on the corridor.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A four-story limit was imposed three years ago; no new office buildings have been built since.

breakdown.analysis: Would anyone have built an office there anyway? If the answer is no, then zero new buildings is exactly what you'd expect with or without the rezoning, and the rezoning gets no blame. Any time an argument blames an action for an outcome, it assumes the outcome wouldn't have happened without that action. Think of a defense lawyer: 'It would have happened anyway.' We need the answer that shuts that defense down. Test by negation.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: without the rezoning, still no office building would likely have been built. Then the empty corridor says nothing about the rezoning, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: Even had the corridor not been rezoned, it is likely that no new office building would have been built along it during the past three years.

choices.note: Too strong. Negate it: maybe only some developers prefer taller buildings. The rezoning could still discourage those developers, so the argument survives.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most developers prefer to build office buildings taller than four stories.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Residential construction tells us nothing required about office development. Negate it (some homes were built) and the office argument is unaffected.
choices.negation: At least one new residential building has been built along the corridor since the rezoning.

choices.note: Tempting, since it hints that tall buildings were wanted there. But negate it: no tall office building was ever built there. Developers might still have planned one now. The argument doesn't need a precedent.
choices.negation: Before the rezoning, no office building taller than four stories had been built along the corridor.

choices.note: Tempting, because a slump in demand is the obvious alternative cause. But 'not declined at all' is far too strong. Negate it: demand dipped slightly. A small dip could leave plenty of demand for a new building, so the argument stands.
choices.negation: Demand for office space in the city has declined at least somewhat over the past three years.

questions.stimulus: Every tree removed from the Wexley greenbelt this year was inspected beforehand by the county arborist. The elm by the footbridge was not removed this year, so the arborist must not have inspected it.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every player who scored a goal for the Hawks this season attended every practice. Dev did not attend every practice, so he did not score a goal for the Hawks this season.
Every dish on the café's menu that contains nuts is marked with a star. The lentil soup is marked with a star, so it must contain nuts.
Only employees who completed safety training were assigned to the night shift. Rosa was assigned to the night shift, so she must have completed safety training.
Every apartment at Elm Court that was repainted this year was also inspected. Unit 4 was inspected this year, so it was probably repainted.
Only paintings that had been appraised beforehand were sold at the Corvin auction. The Varn landscape went unsold at the auction, so no one appraised it beforehand.
questions.explanation: The argument has the form 'every R was I; X was not R; so X was not I,' which wrongly negates a conditional. (E) has the same form in disguise: 'only appraised paintings were sold' means every sold painting was appraised, and it then infers 'not appraised' from 'not sold.' (A) is the most attractive trap because it looks nearly identical on the surface, but it validly uses the contrapositive (not I, so not R); (B) and (D) commit a different flaw, inferring R from I.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The arborist didn't inspect the elm.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every tree removed this year was inspected first; the elm wasn't removed.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All R are I; X is not R; so X is not I. (Removed → Inspected; not Removed; therefore not Inspected.)

breakdown.analysis: Can a tree be inspected and then left standing? Of course. Inspection might have found it healthy. Removed → Inspected only tells you about removed trees; it says nothing about trees that stayed. Concluding not-Inspected from not-Removed negates the rule without flipping it, a classic error. The only valid move is the contrapositive: not Inspected → not Removed. Translate each choice into arrows and look for: A → B; not A; so not B. Beware: 'Only B are A' means A → B, so the matching answer may be written with 'only.'

choices.note: Tempting, because the wording looks almost identical to the stimulus. But map it: Scored → Attended every practice; Dev didn't attend; so he didn't score. That's not B → not A, the valid contrapositive. The stimulus is flawed; this one isn't.
Nuts → Star; soup has a star; so nuts. That's B → A, affirming the consequent. A flaw, but a different one from the stimulus.
'Only trained employees were assigned' means Night shift → Trained. Rosa was on the night shift, so she was trained. That's valid: a straight application of the rule.
Repainted → Inspected; Unit 4 inspected; so probably repainted. That's B → A again (affirming the consequent), softened with 'probably.' Different flaw.

CORRECT. 'Only appraised paintings were sold' means Sold → Appraised. The landscape wasn't sold, so it wasn't appraised: not A → not B. Same flaw as the stimulus, just dressed up with 'only.' An unsold painting could easily have been appraised and then failed to find a buyer.

questions.stimulus: Editor: Two years ago our newspaper began requiring that every story be reviewed by a second editor before publication. Since then, the number of corrections we have had to print each month has fallen by a third. So the policy has made our reporting substantially more accurate.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the editor's argument?
choices: Second editors at the paper sometimes disagree with reporters about how a story should be worded and must then consult a senior editor.
Since the policy began, a much larger share of the paper's corrections have concerned substantive errors rather than minor ones such as misspelled names.
Newspapers in the region that did not adopt a second-editor policy printed about as many corrections per month as they had before.
The review policy has delayed the publication of some stories by several hours, allowing rival outlets to report them first.
Some readers who notice errors in the newspaper do not report them to the paper.
questions.explanation: The editor measures accuracy by the number of corrections, but a third fewer corrections could hide more serious errors; (B) shows the remaining errors are far weightier, so accuracy may not have improved substantially. (E) is tempting, but unreported errors are nothing new and would only matter if reporting had dropped since the policy began. (C) supports the policy’s effect: papers without it saw no drop, which rules out a regional trend.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The second-editor policy has made the paper's reporting substantially more accurate.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the policy began, monthly corrections have fallen by a third.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of corrections really the measure of accuracy? One correction that says a story got the facts backward can outweigh ten misspelled names. If the paper now makes fewer small errors but more big ones, it isn't more accurate in any meaningful way. We need an answer that brings in severity, not just counts.

choices.note: So? Disagreements about wording are part of any review. This doesn't tell us whether accuracy improved.

CORRECT. Fewer corrections, but a much bigger share are about substance. The number of serious errors may have held steady or risen, so the drop in the count doesn't show substantially more accurate reporting.
This strengthens the argument. Papers without the policy saw no drop, so the decline at this paper probably isn’t a regional trend. Wrong direction.
Wrong dimension: speed. Delays don't bear on whether the stories are more accurate.

Tempting, because it suggests the correction count misses some errors. But readers have always failed to report some errors. Unless underreporting increased after the policy began, this doesn't explain the drop.

questions.stimulus: Immunologist: Only vaccines that contain no live virus can safely be given to patients whose immune systems are suppressed, and every patient who has received an organ transplant within the past year has a suppressed immune system. It follows that the newly approved Velmar vaccine contains no live virus.
questions.stem: The immunologist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any vaccine that contains no live virus can safely be given to patients whose immune systems are suppressed.
Most patients whose immune systems are suppressed have received an organ transplant within the past year.
The Velmar vaccine can safely be given to at least some patients whose immune systems are not suppressed.
The Velmar vaccine can safely be given to at least some patients who have received an organ transplant within the past year.
No vaccine that contains live virus has ever been approved for use in organ transplant patients.
questions.explanation: The premises chain: recent transplant → suppressed immune system, and safe for a suppressed patient → no live virus; (D) gives the missing start of the chain, that Velmar is safe for some recent transplant patient, which forces 'no live virus.' (A) is the tempting reversal (no live virus → safe), which says nothing about Velmar. (E) is attractive, but nothing says Velmar was approved for transplant patients.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Velmar contains no live virus.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Safe for a suppressed patient → no live virus; recent transplant → suppressed.

breakdown.analysis: Where does Velmar enter the chain? Nowhere: the premises never mention it. Lay it out: Recent transplant → Suppressed; Safe for a suppressed patient → No live virus. Chain: Safe for a recent transplant patient → (that patient is suppressed) → No live virus. So we need Velmar to be safe for at least one recent transplant patient. Warning: 'Only no-live-virus vaccines are safe' means Safe → No live virus, not the reverse.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses all the right words. But it reverses the first premise: No live virus → Safe. It still never tells us anything about Velmar.
This reverses the second premise (Suppressed → mostly transplant) and still doesn't mention Velmar. No link to the conclusion.
Wrong group. Patients with normal immune systems aren't covered by the 'only' rule, so being safe for them tells us nothing about live virus.

CORRECT. If Velmar is safe for some recent transplant patient, that patient has a suppressed immune system, and only no-live-virus vaccines are safe for such patients. So Velmar contains no live virus.
Tempting, but it only helps if Velmar was approved for transplant patients, which nobody says. Velmar could be approved only for other people.

questions.stimulus: The cleaning robots in the Ferro warehouse are programmed never to drive onto any area of floor that their shared map marks as wet, and they have never been known to disobey this programming. The map marks an area as wet whenever the cleaning crew reports having mopped it. Yesterday, one of the robots drove onto a wet area of floor and slipped.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Yesterday, the cleaning crew mopped at least one area of floor without reporting that it had done so.
Yesterday, some area of the warehouse floor became wet for a reason other than mopping.
Yesterday, the robots' map did not mark as wet every area of the floor that was in fact wet.
The robots cannot sense whether an area of floor is wet except by consulting their shared map.
The robots' map sometimes continues to mark areas as wet after they have dried.
questions.explanation: Robots never drive onto areas marked wet, yet one drove onto a wet area, so that area was wet but not marked: the map missed at least one wet area (C). (A) and (B) are the attractive traps: each offers one way the map could have missed it (an unreported mopping or a spill), but the facts don't tell us which, so neither is supported over the other. (D) is unsupported, since the robots could sense wetness and still be programmed only to avoid marked areas.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Robots never drive onto areas the map marks wet (and have never been known to disobey); 2. the map marks an area wet whenever the crew reports mopping it; 3. yesterday a robot drove onto a wet area and slipped.

breakdown.analysis: If robots never enter marked-wet areas, how did one end up on a wet area? Because that area wasn't marked. Facts 1 and 3 force that much. Why wasn't it marked? Maybe the crew mopped and didn't report it; maybe something spilled; maybe the map glitched. The facts can't tell us. This is a classic existence inference: X happens, Y avoids marked X, so there's unmarked X. Watch for answers that pick one cause when the facts only prove the gap exists.

choices.note: Tempting, because an unreported mopping is a natural story. But the wet patch could have come from a spill or a leak. We don't know it was mopped at all.
Also tempting, as the other natural story. But the area could have been mopped by a crew that forgot to report it. The facts don't pick between A and B.
CORRECT. The robot drove onto a wet area, and robots don't drive onto marked-wet areas. So that wet area wasn't marked. Whatever the reason, the map missed at least one wet area.
We don't know this. The robots may sense wetness perfectly well; they're just programmed to avoid areas the map marks. The facts don't tell us what else they can sense.
This is the reverse problem: marked but dry. Nothing in the facts suggests the map over-marks. The problem yesterday was a wet area that went unmarked.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Advocates of Corvex lozenges claim that the lozenges shorten the common cold. Their only evidence is a trial in which people who took the lozenges recovered faster than people who did not. But in that trial, the people given the lozenges were also told to drink extra fluids, and the others were not. So Corvex lozenges do not shorten the common cold.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that the advocates may have further evidence that the lozenges shorten colds
presumes that the results of a single trial must hold for everyone who catches a cold
attacks the motives of the lozenges' advocates rather than addressing their evidence
takes for granted that drinking extra fluids shortens the common cold
treats the advocates' failure to establish their claim as a demonstration that the claim is false
questions.explanation: The columnist shows that the trial can't separate the lozenges' effect from the fluids' effect, which leaves the advocates' claim unproven, not disproven; the lozenges might still work (E). (D) is the tempting trap: to undermine the trial the columnist needs only that fluids might shorten colds, not that they do. (A) is contradicted by the stimulus, which says the trial is their only evidence, and (B) describes the advocates' leap rather than the columnist's.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Corvex lozenges don't shorten colds.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The advocates' only evidence is a trial in which the lozenge group was also told to drink extra fluids.

breakdown.analysis: So the trial was confounded. Does that prove the lozenges don't work? No. It proves the trial doesn't show that they do. Knocking out someone's evidence leaves their claim unsupported, not false. It's like saying: my friend's proof that it will rain tomorrow was bad, so it won't rain. This is a classic: rebutting an argument isn't the same as disproving its conclusion. We need an answer that says the columnist treats 'not proven' as 'false.'

choices.note: Tempting, since overlooking other evidence is a common flaw. But the stimulus says the trial is the advocates' only evidence, so there's nothing the columnist overlooked.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The one study I read on this vitamin found no effect, so no evidence for the vitamin exists.

choices.note: This describes what the advocates might do, not what the columnist does. The columnist doesn't generalize from the trial at all.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Lozenges helped the people in one trial, so they'll help everyone who catches a cold.

choices.note: The columnist addresses the evidence directly and never mentions motives.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The lozenge advocates are paid by Corvex, so their claims can be ignored.

choices.note: Tempting, because the fluids are the columnist's whole point. But the rebuttal only needs fluids to be a possible cause; that's enough to make the trial inconclusive. The columnist doesn't need to assume fluids actually work.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The lozenge group recovered faster, and they drank extra fluids, so fluids are what cured them.

choices.note: CORRECT. Showing the trial is confounded means the claim hasn't been established. The columnist jumps from there to 'the lozenges don't work,' treating lack of proof as disproof.

questions.stimulus: Newspaper editor: One of our photographers took a picture of a city council member leaving a clinic that treats addiction. We will not publish it. The council member's treatment has no bearing on how she carries out her public duties, and publishing the photograph would cause her and her family considerable distress.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the newspaper editor's decision?
choices: A news organization should not publish information about an official's private life that is irrelevant to the official's public duties and would cause someone significant harm.
A news organization should publish information about a public official's private life whenever that information is accurate and was obtained legally.
Information that is relevant to a public official's duties should always be published, regardless of the distress its publication may cause.
News organizations should avoid publishing photographs of people that were taken without the knowledge or consent of the person photographed.
Whether to publish information about a public official should depend solely on how much interest the public would have in that information.
questions.explanation: The editor gives two reasons, irrelevance to public duties and serious distress, and (A) says that when both hold, the information should not be published, which is exactly the editor's decision. (D) is tempting, but nothing says the photograph was taken without the council member's knowledge or consent, and the editor doesn't rely on that. (C) tells us what to do with relevant information, which this photograph isn't.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The paper will not publish the photo of the council member leaving the clinic.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Her treatment is irrelevant to her public duties; publishing would cause her and her family considerable distress.

breakdown.analysis: What rule turns those two reasons into 'don't publish'? A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, using the facts you've got. Here: irrelevant to duties + causes harm → don't publish. We need a principle with exactly that shape.

choices.note: CORRECT. Both conditions are met: the treatment is irrelevant to her duties, and publication would cause significant distress. The principle then says don't publish, which is the editor's decision.
This points the other way. If the photo was accurate and legally taken, this principle says publish.
This covers relevant information. The editor says this information is irrelevant, so the principle doesn't apply and can't justify the decision.
Tempting, since it would block publishing. But we don't know the photo was taken without her knowledge or consent, and the editor's reasons are about relevance and harm, not consent.
Wrong dimension: public interest. And the public might be very curious, which could push toward publishing. It doesn't support the decision.

questions.stimulus: Forester: Most of the young saplings lost in the Corran Forest each year are eaten by deer; only a small fraction are trampled by hikers. So the proposal to close the forest's trails to hikers each spring will not substantially reduce the number of saplings lost each year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the forester's argument?
choices: Most of the noise complaints in Ellery come from residents who live near the airport rather than near the highway. So the noise in Ellery is worse near the airport than near the highway.
Most of the traffic accidents in Pell occur on weekends. So the plan to add police patrols on weekends will substantially reduce the number of traffic accidents in Pell.
Most of the books returned late to the Hadley library are children's books. So the library should extend the loan period for children's books.
Most of the water lost from the Halston reservoir evaporates; only a little leaks through the old dam. So repairing the dam will not substantially reduce the amount of water the reservoir loses.
Most of the trees in Ardell Park are oaks, and most oaks lose their leaves in the fall. So most of the trees in Ardell Park lose their leaves in the fall.
questions.explanation: The forester reasons that because a proposal addresses only a minor cause of a loss, it won't substantially reduce the loss; (D) does the same with a dam repair that addresses only the minor cause of water loss. (B) is tempting because it also concerns a plan aimed at a share of a problem, but it targets the main share and concludes the plan will work. (E) is a quantifier argument with no plan or causes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Closing the trails to hikers in spring won't substantially reduce sapling losses.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most sapling losses come from deer; only a small fraction come from hikers.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most of loss L comes from cause A; only a little comes from cause B; so a plan that addresses only B won't substantially reduce L.

breakdown.analysis: Strip it down: two causes of a problem, one big and one small; the proposal tackles only the small one; so it won't make a big dent. Match every piece: a loss, a major cause, a minor cause, a plan aimed at the minor cause, and a 'won't substantially reduce' conclusion.

choices.note: No plan and no causes of a loss. It moves from where complaints come from to where noise is worse. Different structure.
Tempting, because it has a 'most' and a plan. But the plan targets the main share and concludes it will work. That's the reverse of the forester's 'targets the minor share, won't work.'
Ends in a recommendation ('should extend'), and the plan targets the major share. Different conclusion type.
CORRECT. Major cause (evaporation), minor cause (leaks), plan addresses only the minor one (repair the dam), so it won't substantially reduce the loss. Piece for piece the same.
A 'most + most' quantifier chain about trees. No plan, no causes, no reduction. Completely different (and flawed) structure.

questions.stimulus: Arts columnist: Every member of the Brightwater Youth Orchestra has won top honors at a state solo competition, whereas few members of the rival Kessel Youth Orchestra have ever placed at such a competition, though most have entered. Clearly, then, the Brightwater orchestra performs better as an ensemble than the Kessel orchestra does.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the arts columnist's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: takes for granted that state solo competitions are judged fairly
presumes that an orchestra whose members are better soloists must perform better as an ensemble
draws a conclusion about all youth orchestras from a comparison of only two
overlooks the possibility that some Kessel members have won honors at competitions in other states
relies on the judgments of competition judges, who may lack expertise in orchestral playing
questions.explanation: The evidence is about the members' individual solo achievements, but the conclusion is about how each orchestra performs as a group; ensemble playing depends on more than the sum of soloists' skills (B). (E) is tempting because it hints that solo judges aren't judging ensembles, but the columnist relies on them only for solo skill, which is what they judged; the problem is the jump from parts to whole. (A) is merely possible.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Brightwater performs better as an ensemble than Kessel.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All Brightwater members won top solo honors; few Kessel members have placed.

breakdown.analysis: Do great soloists automatically make a great orchestra? Not necessarily. Ensemble playing takes listening, blending, and following a conductor. A team of star players isn't always the best team. This is the part-to-whole flaw (composition): what's true of each member isn't automatically true of the group. It's a classic; know it. We need an answer that names the jump from individual skill to group performance.

choices.note: Merely possible. Nothing suggests the competitions are unfair, and even with perfect judging, solo skill wouldn't guarantee ensemble quality.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Kim won the essay contest, so she must be the best writer in the school (ignoring that the judges might have played favorites).

choices.note: CORRECT. Solo honors are a fact about individual members; ensemble performance is a fact about the group. Assuming the group inherits its members' strengths is the composition flaw.
The conclusion compares just these two orchestras. There's no claim about youth orchestras in general.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Brightwater outplays Kessel, so orchestras with prizewinning members always outplay other orchestras.

choices.note: Merely possible, and it doesn't fix the real problem. Even if Kessel members won honors elsewhere, the jump from solo skill to ensemble skill would remain.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: No Kessel member placed at our state competition, so no Kessel member has ever won anything.

choices.note: Tempting, because it gestures at the solo-vs.-ensemble difference. But the judges assessed solo playing, and the columnist uses their verdicts only as evidence of solo skill. The judges' expertise isn't the gap; the leap from soloists to ensemble is.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: A famous violinist says the school's new math curriculum is excellent, so it must be.

passages.title: Poets’ recordings of their own work
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Passage A

When a poet records a reading of his or her own work, the recording preserves something the printed page cannot: the poet’s own sense of how the lines should move. Print fixes the words but leaves much of their timing open. A reader confronting an irregular line must decide where the stresses fall, how long to pause at a line break, and whether a dash marks a hesitation or a rush. On such matters the poet’s voice is the best evidence we will ever have.

Consider the case of Hedda Morrow, whose 1958 collection Tidewater was long faulted for its “shapeless” free verse. Critics who knew the poems only from the page heard no pattern in them. Yet in the recordings Morrow made for a regional radio station in 1960, she reads nearly every line with four strong beats, pausing so deliberately at the ends of lines that the apparent shapelessness disappears. The pattern was there all along; the page simply failed to show it.

Scholars who interpret a poem’s rhythm without consulting the poet’s recordings, where such recordings exist, therefore proceed with less than the full evidence. An edition of Morrow’s poems ought to direct readers to her readings, and any account of her prosody that ignores them should be regarded as provisional at best. The poet’s recorded voice is not merely one performance among many; it is the closest thing we have to a score.

Passage B

Archives now hold thousands of recordings of poets reading their own work, and scholars have begun to treat these recordings as keys to the sound of the poems. The recordings are invaluable, but they deserve more caution than they usually receive.

A poet reading aloud is a performer, and performances answer to circumstance. Calloway Ness recorded his poem “Harbor Psalm” three times over twenty years: slowly and evenly in 1949, briskly in 1957, and in 1968, before a large audience, with long dramatic pauses that appear in neither earlier version. Which of these is the poem’s true rhythm? To privilege any one of them is to choose, not to discover. Nor is a poet necessarily a skilled reader. Some poets have admitted to reading in a flat, hurried manner they find uncomfortable to hear, and nervousness before a microphone may alter a reading in ways that have nothing to do with the verse.

Moreover, a published poem addresses readers who will never hear the poet’s voice, and the page has resources of its own—line breaks, spacing, punctuation—that the poet chose deliberately. When a recording seems to override these, it is at least as plausible that the poet was improvising as that the page was deficient.

None of this makes recordings irrelevant. A reading documents one way a poem was understood by someone who knew it intimately, and it can alert us to possibilities we would otherwise miss. But it is evidence to be weighed, not a verdict to be obeyed.

passages.title: Brandt and the end of Halvern’s volunteer fire companies
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Through most of the nineteenth century, the towns of the Halvern province relied for protection against fire on volunteer companies: associations of tradesmen and shopkeepers who drilled together, maintained a hand-drawn engine, and answered the alarm bell without pay. Between 1870 and 1900 nearly all of these companies were disbanded and replaced by salaried municipal departments. The standard explanation holds that the volunteers simply could not keep pace with the growth of the towns: as buildings rose higher and streets multiplied, fires outstripped what part-time crews could control.

The historian Anika Brandt finds this explanation unpersuasive. Volunteer companies, she notes, were often quick to acquire new equipment, including steam-powered pumps, and municipal records give little indication that fire losses in Halvern’s towns rose in the years before the changeover. What changed, in Brandt’s view, was the market for fire insurance. As large insurers based in the provincial capital extended their business into the smaller towns, they began setting premiums according to the kind of protection a town provided, and they offered substantially lower rates in towns that maintained a paid department. Merchants and property owners—the very people who filled the volunteer ranks—thus acquired a direct financial interest in abolishing their own companies.

Brandt’s account has the considerable merit of explaining the timing of the change, which the standard view leaves obscure: in town after town, the disbanding of the volunteer company followed the arrival of the large insurers, sometimes within a few years. It also explains why, as council minutes show, members of the volunteer companies themselves frequently proposed the measures that ended their companies.

Yet the account leaves an important question unanswered: why did the insurers prefer paid departments? Brandt treats the insurers’ rate schedules as though they simply recorded a judgment about which kind of department fought fires better—but she has herself argued that there is little evidence the volunteers fought fires worse. If the insurers’ preference was not grounded in performance, it may have rested on something else: perhaps the fact that a salaried department, answerable to a town council, could be held to written standards of readiness, whereas a volunteer company’s obligations were matters of custom and honor. Such an explanation would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim, but it would shift its emphasis, locating the decisive change not in the insurance market as such but in a broader preference, shared by insurers and councils alike, for obligations that could be specified and enforced.

Nor does Brandt account for the handful of towns, such as Orrisby, that kept their volunteer companies into the 1910s despite paying higher premiums. Until such exceptions are explained, her account, though a considerable improvement on its predecessor, cannot be regarded as complete.

passages.title: Ferreira on the Dolan test for suggestive identifications
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
