In the courts of Calvery, an eyewitness identification obtained through a suggestive police procedure—showing the witness a single suspect rather than a lineup, for example, or telling the witness after a selection that she has picked the right person—is not automatically excluded from trial. Under the rule announced in Regina v. Dolan (1979), a judge who finds a procedure unnecessarily suggestive must nonetheless admit the identification if, considering all the circumstances, it appears reliable. Among the circumstances the court listed were the witness’s opportunity to view the offender, the attention the witness paid, and the certainty the witness expresses in the identification.

The legal scholar Anouk Ferreira has argued that the Dolan test defeats itself, because its reliability factors are not independent of the suggestion they are meant to offset. Research on memory has established that a witness who receives confirming feedback after choosing someone (“Good, you identified our suspect”) typically becomes more confident in the choice and, asked later, tends to report having had a better view and having paid closer attention than witnesses who received no such feedback. A suggestive procedure can thus inflate the very measures a court consults to decide whether the suggestion did harm, so that the worse the procedure, the more reliable the resulting identification may appear. The test, in Ferreira’s phrase, is “a thermometer that the fever itself can reset.” She concludes that any identification obtained through an unnecessarily suggestive procedure should be excluded.

Ferreira’s diagnosis is difficult to resist. A witness’s certainty as stated on the stand, months after the procedure and after repeated retelling of the account, tells a court more about what has happened to the witness’s memory since the identification than about the identification itself. But her remedy sweeps more broadly than her diagnosis requires. Excluding every such identification would discard some that are very likely accurate—that of a witness who picks a longtime neighbor out of a fair lineup as the offender, for instance, and is then told that she has chosen the suspect. And her argument shows only that the Dolan factors, as courts now measure them, are contaminated; it does not show that no uncontaminated measure exists.

Suppose police were required to record, in the witness’s own words, how confident the witness was and how well she had seen and attended to the offender, at the moment of the first identification and before any feedback could be given. That record would be fixed before the confirming remarks Ferreira describes could act on it, and a court could consult it in place of the witness’s later testimony. Admittedly, such a record would not cure every suggestive procedure: a witness shown a single suspect is steered toward a choice before any confidence can be stated, and for procedures of that kind Ferreira’s strictness may well be warranted. But for the distortion on which her critique chiefly rests, a reformed test, not exclusion, is the proportionate response.

passages.title: Winged seeds in Tessel’s campion
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Tessel’s campion, a low perennial of the Merrow uplands, bears two kinds of seed: heavy, smooth seeds that fall close to the parent and lighter seeds fringed with a papery wing that the wind can carry tens of meters. Botanists long assumed that the winged seeds served chiefly to carry the species into newly opened ground, such as the rockfalls common on the uplands’ steeper slopes. A 1998 survey by the botanist Ruth Aldane therefore came as a puzzle. Aldane found that plants on steep, frequently disturbed slopes devoted only about 15 percent of their seeds to the winged form, whereas plants in the dense, stable meadows of the valley floors, where open ground is scarce, devoted nearly half.

Aldane’s explanation centered on competition among relatives. In a crowded meadow, a seed that falls beside its parent must compete for one of a few small gaps in the turf, and its most likely competitors are its own siblings. Suppose a parent drops forty heavy seeds into the turf around it and two gaps open there in a season: at most two of the forty can establish, and the rest are lost. A winged seed that lands elsewhere competes mostly with the offspring of other plants, so each one that reaches a gap adds to the parent’s descendants rather than replacing a sibling that would have taken the gap anyway. On a disturbed slope the arithmetic is different: open ground near the parent is plentiful, and the parent’s own survival shows the immediate site to be suitable, so heavy seeds dropped nearby are seldom wasted.

Aldane’s account implied that the plants could detect crowding. In a greenhouse, she raised seedlings from both habitats in pots at high and low densities. Plants grown crowded produced a high proportion of winged seeds and plants grown sparsely a low one, regardless of whether their parents had come from meadow or slope. The difference between the habitats, then, was not inherited but a response to the conditions each plant encountered.

How the plants sense crowding was clarified in 2010 by Tomas Ferrel. Leaves absorb red light strongly but transmit and reflect much of the far-red, so light that has passed through or bounced off neighboring foliage is relatively poor in red. Growing campion without neighbors under adjustable lamps, Ferrel found that a low ratio of red to far-red light alone raised the proportion of winged seeds to meadow levels, whereas merely dimming the lamps had no effect. Yet the cue is imperfect. Campion growing beneath young birch on the slopes, where the canopy filters the light but the ground below is open and gaps are plentiful, produces winged seeds in meadow proportions.

Aldane’s account has held up well, but such cases suggest a refinement: the campion responds not to crowding itself but to a signal that ordinarily accompanies crowding, and where the two come apart, the plant’s allocation may serve it poorly. Whether the birch-shaded plants actually suffer for it has yet to be measured.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A describes a scholarly practice without evaluating it; passage B argues that the practice should be abandoned.
Passage A argues that a certain kind of evidence is unreliable; passage B argues that the same kind of evidence is the best available.
Passage A gives a historical account of how a kind of evidence came to be valued; passage B offers further examples that support that account.
Passage A argues that a certain kind of evidence should be treated as authoritative; passage B grants the value of that kind of evidence but argues that it should not be treated as decisive.
Passage A and passage B each criticize a different kind of evidence used in determining the rhythm of a poem.
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that a poet’s recorded reading is ‘the best evidence we will ever have’ and ‘the closest thing we have to a score’; passage B calls such recordings ‘invaluable’ but insists they are ‘evidence to be weighed, not a verdict to be obeyed.’ That is D. B reverses the two positions, and A misdescribes both passages: A is plainly evaluative, and passage B never says recordings should be set aside.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Label each passage’s stance toward poets’ recordings, then match the pair.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of passage A and the first and last paragraphs of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: Do the two passages really fight? Not completely. A: the poet’s recording is the authority on rhythm. B: recordings are “invaluable,” but they’re just evidence, “not a verdict.” So we want: A treats something as authoritative; B accepts its value but denies it the final word. A partial disagreement, not a flat rejection.

choices.note: Passage A isn’t neutral; it says criticism that ignores recordings is “provisional at best.” And passage B never says to abandon recordings. Its last paragraph says the opposite: “None of this makes recordings irrelevant.”
This flips the two passages. A is the one that says recordings are the best evidence; B is the more cautious one.
Passage A isn’t a history of how recordings came to be valued; it’s an argument that they should be. And B doesn’t support A, it qualifies it.
CORRECT. A: the recording is “the closest thing we have to a score.” B: it’s “invaluable” but “evidence to be weighed, not a verdict to be obeyed.” Grants the value, denies the authority.
Both passages are about the same kind of evidence: the poet’s own recorded reading. And A doesn’t criticize it at all.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: the printed text of a poem leaves some aspects of the poem’s rhythm undetermined
an account of a poem’s rhythm that conflicts with the poet’s own recorded reading should for that reason be regarded as doubtful
a recording of a poet reading his or her own work can call a reader’s attention to features of a poem that might otherwise go unnoticed
the poems in Hedda Morrow’s Tidewater follow a regular pattern of stresses
poets who record the same poem more than once sometimes read it in noticeably different ways
questions.explanation: Passage A holds that an account of a poet’s prosody that ignores the poet’s readings is ‘provisional at best,’ because the recording is the best evidence of rhythm; passage B holds that when a recording seems to override the page, the poet may simply have been improvising, so the recording is not a verdict. That is B. A is tempting because passage A asserts it, but passage B never denies that print leaves some timing open. D and E are each addressed by only one passage, and both authors would accept C.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim one author would affirm and the other would deny.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A’s third paragraph; passage B’s third and fourth paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. Silence doesn’t count. Where do they clash? A: ignore the poet’s recording and your account is “provisional at best.” B: a recording that seems to override the page may just be improvisation; weigh it, don’t obey it. So they split on whether the recording gets to overrule other readings.

choices.note: Tempting, because passage A says it outright (“Print fixes the words but leaves much of their timing open”). But B never denies it. B says the page has resources of its own, not that it settles everything. B even says recordings can show us possibilities we’d miss, which suggests the page leaves some things open.

CORRECT. A: yes, the recording is the best evidence, so an account that conflicts with it is suspect. B: no, the recording is “evidence to be weighed, not a verdict to be obeyed”; the poet may have been improvising.
Both would agree. A’s Morrow example is exactly this, and B says a reading “can alert us to possibilities we would otherwise miss.”
Only passage A discusses Morrow. B says nothing about Tidewater, so we can’t say B would deny it.
Only passage B makes this point (the three readings of “Harbor Psalm”). Passage A never addresses repeated recordings, so there’s no disagreement on record.

questions.stem: The author of passage B discusses the three recordings of “Harbor Psalm” (second paragraph of passage B) primarily in order to
choices: show that recordings made before large audiences are less reliable than recordings made in private
illustrate the claim that some poets are not skilled readers of their own work
suggest that a poet’s understanding of a poem’s rhythm grows more accurate over time
demonstrate that the printed text of “Harbor Psalm” fails to indicate the poem’s intended rhythm
support the contention that a poet’s readings are shaped by circumstance and so do not identify a single authoritative rhythm
questions.explanation: The example comes right after ‘performances answer to circumstance’ and is followed by ‘To privilege any one of them is to choose, not to discover.’ Three different readings of one poem show that no single reading can be treated as the poem’s true rhythm, which is E. B is the tempting trap: it describes the next point (‘Nor is a poet necessarily a skilled reader’), which the passage introduces as a separate consideration.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why passage B brings up Ness’s three recordings.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph of passage B: the sentence before the example and the two sentences after it.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sandwich. Before: “performances answer to circumstance.” After: “Which of these is the poem’s true rhythm? To privilege any one of them is to choose, not to discover.” So the example shows that readings vary with the occasion, and so no one reading is the authoritative one. We want an answer that says that.

choices.note: Too specific. The 1968 reading happened to be before a large audience, but B never ranks audience recordings against private ones. The point is variation, not which setting is better.
Tempting, because it’s in the same paragraph. But “Nor is a poet necessarily a skilled reader” starts a new, separate point. Nothing suggests Ness read badly; his readings just differed.
We don’t know this. B never says the later readings are more accurate; if anything, it refuses to pick one as “true.”
The example is about the recordings, not the printed text. B actually defends the page’s own resources in the next paragraph.
CORRECT. Three readings, three rhythms, depending on the occasion. That’s the support for “performances answer to circumstance” and for the claim that picking one is choosing, not discovering.

questions.stem: Based on passage B, its author would most likely respond to passage A’s discussion of Hedda Morrow’s recordings (second paragraph of passage A) by pointing out that
choices: the deliberate pauses at the ends of lines in Morrow’s 1960 readings may reflect the circumstances of that performance rather than a pattern present in the poems themselves
Morrow probably did not compose the poems in Tidewater with any regular pattern of stresses in mind
the critics who considered Tidewater shapeless had evidently relied on Morrow’s recordings rather than on the printed poems
a radio broadcast is an unsuitable occasion for a poet to read his or her own work aloud
Morrow’s recordings should be disregarded by anyone attempting to describe the rhythm of the poems in Tidewater
questions.explanation: Passage B argues that readings ‘answer to circumstance’ and that when a recording seems to override the page, ‘it is at least as plausible that the poet was improvising as that the page was deficient.’ Applied to Morrow, that yields A’s hedged point: the pauses may belong to the performance, not the poems. B is the strongest trap, but passage B claims only that improvisation is at least as plausible, not that it is probable, and it says nothing about what Morrow had in mind when composing. E is too strong, since passage B insists recordings are not irrelevant.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply passage B’s cautions to passage A’s Morrow example.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph; passage B, second and third paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A reads Morrow’s 1960 radio readings as proof that “the pattern was there all along.” What would B say? B’s third paragraph is built for this case: when a recording seems to override the page, “it is at least as plausible that the poet was improvising as that the page was deficient.” So B would say: maybe the four beats and the pauses came from that one performance. Watch the strength. B only says “at least as plausible,” so the right answer must be hedged.

choices.note: CORRECT. It’s passage B’s general warning applied to Morrow, at the right strength (“may reflect”). The pauses could belong to the 1960 occasion rather than to the poems.
Tempting, because it sounds like B’s skepticism. But it’s too strong. B says improvisation is “at least as plausible,” not more likely. And B says nothing about what a poet intended while composing.
Backwards. Passage A says these critics “knew the poems only from the page.” B gives no reason to doubt that.
B never says some occasions are unsuitable for readings. The issue is how much weight a reading gets, not where it was made.
Too strong. B’s last paragraph says “None of this makes recordings irrelevant.” Weigh them, yes; disregard them, no.

questions.stem: In describing the poet’s recorded voice as ‘the closest thing we have to a score’ (last sentence of passage A), the author of passage A most probably means that the recording
choices: is, like a musical score, consulted mainly by specialists rather than by general readers
shows that a poem, like a piece of music, cannot be appreciated unless it is heard aloud
comes nearer than any other available source to specifying how the lines of the poem are meant to be timed and stressed
should, like a musical score, be revised by later performers whenever it proves inadequate
indicates that poets ought to set their verse to music in order to preserve its rhythm
questions.explanation: A score tells performers how a piece is to be timed and stressed. Passage A has argued that print ‘leaves much of their timing open’ and that the poet’s voice is ‘the best evidence’ about stresses and pauses; calling the recording the closest thing to a score means it comes nearest to fixing that timing, which is C. B is the tempting trap: it picks up the musical comparison, but passage A never claims poems must be heard to be appreciated; its point concerns evidence of intended rhythm.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decode the score metaphor.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of passage A, read with the first paragraph’s claim that print leaves timing open.

breakdown.analysis: What does a score do? It tells a performer how the notes are timed and stressed. Passage A’s complaint about print is exactly that it leaves timing open. So calling the recording “the closest thing we have to a score” means: it’s the nearest thing to an instruction sheet for the poem’s rhythm. Note “closest”: A admits it isn’t a perfect score.

choices.note: Wrong feature of a score. A says nothing about who consults recordings; it wants editions to direct all readers to them.
Tempting, because it borrows the music comparison. But A never says a poem can’t be appreciated on the page. Its claim is narrower: the recording is the best evidence of the intended rhythm.
CORRECT. A score specifies timing and stress; print doesn’t; the recording comes closest. That’s A’s whole argument in one image.
Opposite spirit. A wants the recording to govern interpretation, not to be revised by others.
Takes the metaphor literally. A isn’t asking poets to write music; it’s describing what the recording does.

questions.stem: Passage B mentions which one of the following as a factor that may affect a poet’s reading of his or her own work?
choices: the poet’s familiarity with recordings made by other poets
revisions the poet has made to the printed text of the poem
the opinions of critics who have reviewed the poem
the quality of the equipment used to make the recording
nervousness before a microphone
questions.explanation: The second paragraph of passage B says that ‘nervousness before a microphone may alter a reading in ways that have nothing to do with the verse.’ That is E. D is the likeliest slip because it also concerns the recording situation, but passage B never mentions the quality of recording equipment; A, B, and C are likewise never mentioned.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the factor passage B actually names.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Pure detail question. Find the line. Passage B lists things that shape a reading: circumstance and audience (the Ness example), the poet’s skill as a reader, and “nervousness before a microphone.” The right answer will be one of these, nearly word for word.

choices.note: Never mentioned. B says nothing about poets listening to other poets.
Never mentioned. B talks about the page’s line breaks and punctuation, but not about the poet revising the printed text.
Never mentioned. Critics show up in passage A, not as an influence on how a poet reads.
Tempting, since it’s about the recording setup, like the microphone. But B never says anything about equipment quality. Stick to what’s stated.
CORRECT. Stated directly: nervousness before a microphone “may alter a reading in ways that have nothing to do with the verse.”

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument in passage A depends and that the author of passage B calls into question?
choices: The rhythm of a poem is relevant to how the poem should be interpreted.
A poet’s reading of his or her own poem reflects the rhythm the poet intended for it rather than circumstances peculiar to the occasion of the reading.
Readers who never hear a poet read aloud are unable to understand the poet’s poems.
Poems written in free verse are more likely than poems in regular meter to be misread on the page.
Recordings made for radio broadcast are prepared more carefully than recordings made before live audiences.
questions.explanation: Passage A moves from ‘Morrow read the lines with four beats’ to ‘the pattern was there all along,’ which requires that a poet’s reading reflect the intended rhythm rather than the occasion; passage B challenges exactly this with ‘performances answer to circumstance’ and the point about nervousness. That is B. A is required by passage A but passage B accepts it, since B cares about the page’s line breaks and punctuation. C is the strongest trap: passage B does stress readers who never hear the poet, but passage A claims only that accounts ignoring recordings are provisional, not that such readers cannot understand the poems.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim that passage A needs AND that passage B attacks. Both conditions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second and third paragraphs; passage B, second and third paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Two filters, so check every choice twice. Where’s A’s gap? A hears Morrow read four beats and concludes “the pattern was there all along.” So what if she read it that way? That only shows the poem’s pattern if her reading reflects what the poem is, not what that day was like. That’s the assumption. B goes straight at it: “performances answer to circumstance,” nervousness can “alter a reading.” Negation test: if a poet’s reading reflected only the occasion, A’s Morrow argument collapses.

choices.note: Passes the first filter, fails the second. A does need rhythm to matter. But B agrees: it defends line breaks and punctuation because they shape how the poem moves. B never questions this.
CORRECT. A needs it: otherwise Morrow’s 1960 reading proves nothing about the poems. B attacks it: Ness’s three different readings and the nervousness point both show readings tracking the occasion.

Tempting, because B does say a poem “addresses readers who will never hear the poet’s voice,” which sounds like a reply to this. But A never claims such readers can’t understand the poems; it says only that accounts ignoring recordings are provisional. Fails the first filter.
Neither passage compares free verse with metrical verse. Morrow’s free verse is just A’s example.
Neither passage ranks radio recordings against live ones. Morrow’s radio setting and Ness’s audience are incidental details.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Brandt’s explanation of why Halvern’s volunteer fire companies were replaced by paid departments improves on the standard explanation, but it leaves unanswered questions about the insurers’ preference and about towns that kept their volunteers.
The volunteer fire companies of Halvern were disbanded because they could not control the fires that occurred in rapidly growing towns.
The insurers who did business in Halvern’s towns preferred paid fire departments because such departments had been shown to fight fires more effectively than volunteer companies.
Brandt’s explanation of the end of Halvern’s volunteer fire companies is mistaken, because it cannot account for towns such as Orrisby.
The volunteer fire companies of Halvern declined because of a widespread preference among insurers and town councils for obligations that could be specified and enforced.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the standard explanation, Brandt’s insurance-based alternative and its merits, and then two gaps: why insurers preferred paid departments, and towns like Orrisby. A covers all of this. D overstates the author’s criticism: the author calls the account incomplete, not mistaken. E presents the author’s tentative suggestion (‘perhaps’) as the passage’s conclusion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the passage’s main point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First sentence of the second paragraph, first sentence of the third and fourth paragraphs, and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Map it. P1: background plus the standard explanation. P2: Brandt rejects it and offers insurance. P3: what Brandt explains well. P4: a gap (why did insurers prefer paid departments?). P5: another gap (Orrisby), ending “a considerable improvement … cannot be regarded as complete.” That last sentence is basically the main point: better than the old view, but incomplete.

choices.note: CORRECT. Better than its predecessor, plus the two open questions. It matches the last sentence of the passage almost exactly.
That’s the standard explanation, which Brandt rejects and the author doesn’t defend.
Contradicts the passage. Brandt argues there is “little evidence the volunteers fought fires worse,” and the author builds on that.
Too strong. The author says the account is incomplete, “not … complete,” and calls it “a considerable improvement.” Incomplete isn’t mistaken.
Tempting, but this is the author’s “perhaps” suggestion from P4, offered as a possible refinement. It isn’t the passage’s conclusion.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Brandt cites which one of the following as evidence against the standard explanation?
choices: Merchants and property owners made up much of the membership of volunteer companies.
Insurers offered lower premiums to towns that maintained paid departments.
Some towns kept their volunteer companies into the 1910s.
Volunteer companies were often quick to acquire new equipment.
Buildings in Halvern’s towns grew taller during the second half of the nineteenth century.
questions.explanation: Right after calling the standard explanation unpersuasive, Brandt ‘notes’ that volunteer companies ‘were often quick to acquire new equipment, including steam-powered pumps,’ and that fire losses did not seem to rise. That is D. B is the tempting trap: it is a fact Brandt relies on, but as support for her own insurance account, not as evidence against the standard one. C is raised by the author, against Brandt.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Brandt offers against the old view.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Detail, but watch the role. The second paragraph has two jobs: knock down the standard view (sentences 1–2), then build Brandt’s own view (the rest). The stem asks only about the knockdown. Evidence there: volunteers got new equipment fast; fire losses didn’t rise.

choices.note: Part of Brandt’s positive account (the people who had a financial interest were the volunteers themselves), not evidence against the old view.
Tempting, it’s Brandt’s key fact. But it supports her insurance story; it doesn’t show the volunteers could keep pace. Right passage, wrong job.
The author raises Orrisby, and raises it against Brandt.
CORRECT. Stated in the second sentence of the second paragraph. If volunteers kept updating their gear, “they couldn’t keep pace” loses force.
That’s part of the standard explanation itself, not evidence against it.

questions.stem: The primary function of the fourth paragraph is to
choices: present evidence that undermines Brandt’s central claim about the role of the insurance market
argue that the standard explanation of the change was correct after all
identify a tension in Brandt’s account and propose a possible explanation that would refine that account
describe the procedure by which insurers set premiums for the towns of Halvern
establish that volunteer companies fought fires as effectively as paid departments did
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph notes that Brandt treats rate schedules as a judgment about firefighting performance even though she has argued the volunteers did not fight fires worse, and then offers, with ‘perhaps,’ that insurers preferred enforceable written standards; the author says this ‘would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim’ but would shift its emphasis. That is C. A is the tempting trap, but the author expressly says the suggestion is compatible with Brandt’s central claim, so it refines rather than undermines it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the fourth paragraph does in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The whole fourth paragraph, especially “Yet,” “but she has herself argued,” and “would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim.”

breakdown.analysis: Two moves. 1. A tension: Brandt treats the insurers’ rates as a judgment about who fights fires better, but she herself said the volunteers weren’t worse. 2. A fix: maybe insurers liked enforceable written standards. Then the author says the fix is “compatible with Brandt’s central claim” but shifts the emphasis. So: point out a problem, suggest a refinement.

choices.note: Tempting, because the paragraph is critical. But the author says the alternative “would be compatible with Brandt’s central claim.” It refines her account; it doesn’t undermine it.
The standard explanation is never revived. The paragraph actually relies on Brandt’s point that the volunteers weren’t worse.
CORRECT. Tension (performance-based rates vs. no performance gap) plus a possible refinement (enforceable obligations).
The paragraph asks why insurers preferred paid departments; it doesn’t describe how premiums were calculated.
That’s Brandt’s claim from the second paragraph, and even there it’s “little evidence” they were worse, not proof they were equal. The fourth paragraph uses it; it doesn’t establish it.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that the standard explanation would have difficulty accounting for which one of the following?
choices: that the towns of Halvern grew substantially during the second half of the nineteenth century
that in many towns the volunteer company was disbanded within a few years after the large insurers began doing business there
that the volunteer companies were made up largely of tradesmen and shopkeepers
that fires became harder to control as the buildings in Halvern’s towns rose higher
that a few towns kept their volunteer companies despite paying higher insurance premiums
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says Brandt’s account explains ‘the timing of the change, which the standard view leaves obscure,’ namely that disbanding followed the insurers’ arrival, sometimes within a few years. So B is something the standard explanation struggles with. E is the trap: the author raises such towns as a problem for Brandt’s account, not for the standard one, and the standard view could explain them if those towns grew little. A and D are part of the standard explanation itself.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a fact the old “couldn’t keep pace” view can’t explain.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, first sentence: “which the standard view leaves obscure.”

breakdown.analysis: The passage hands you this. The standard view is about growth: bigger towns, taller buildings, too much for volunteers. Why would that line up with when insurers showed up? It wouldn’t. The third paragraph says the timing is something “the standard view leaves obscure.” We want the timing fact.

choices.note: Growth is the standard explanation’s own premise. It explains this easily.
CORRECT. The timing tracks the insurers, not town growth, and the passage says the standard view “leaves obscure” this timing.
Neutral. Who joined the companies doesn’t bear on whether volunteers could keep pace.
Again, this is what the standard explanation claims. No difficulty there.
Tempting, because it’s raised as an unexplained exception. But the author raises Orrisby against Brandt’s account. The standard view could handle it if those towns didn’t grow much. Wrong target.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author’s suggestion in the fourth paragraph about the basis of the insurers’ preference for paid departments?
choices: In towns with paid departments, fires were on average brought under control more quickly than in towns with volunteer companies.
Many volunteer companies in Halvern held annual contests in which crews competed to pump water the farthest.
Insurers generally set a town’s premium before they had observed its fire department respond to any fire.
Town councils in Halvern frequently disputed the premiums that insurers charged to property owners.
Insurers granted the lower premium to any town whose fire department was bound by written regulations on staffing and readiness, including the few volunteer companies that adopted such regulations.
questions.explanation: The author suggests that insurers preferred paid departments not for their performance but because they could be held to written, enforceable standards. E shows that the discount followed written regulations even when the department was volunteer, which isolates exactly that factor. C is the tempting trap: it suggests rates were not based on observed performance, but insurers could still have been relying on assumptions about performance, so it does not point to enforceable standards. A supports a performance basis and so weakens the suggestion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Support the author’s guess about WHY insurers liked paid departments.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, from “If the insurers’ preference was not grounded in performance” to the end.

breakdown.analysis: The author’s hypothesis: insurers liked paid departments because they could be held to written standards, not because they fought fires better. How do you best support a “this factor, not that one” claim? Separate the factors. Find a case where the written-standards factor is present without the paid-department label and see if the discount follows it. We want an answer that ties the discount to enforceable rules themselves.

choices.note: Opposite direction. If paid departments really performed better, the obvious basis for the preference is performance, which is the explanation the author is trying to replace.
Irrelevant. Volunteer pride and pumping contests say nothing about why insurers set rates as they did.

Tempting. It hints that insurers weren’t judging actual performance. But they could still have assumed paid crews were better without watching them. It doesn’t point to written standards at all; at most it clears a little ground.
Irrelevant. Councils arguing over premiums doesn’t tell us what insurers based their preference on.
CORRECT. Volunteer companies with written rules got the discount too. So the discount followed enforceable standards, not the paid label or performance. That’s the author’s hypothesis, isolated.

questions.stem: In describing a volunteer company’s obligations as ‘matters of custom and honor’ (fourth paragraph), the author most likely means that these obligations
choices: were not set down in a form that could be formally enforced
were taken less seriously by volunteers than paid firefighters took their duties
were passed down from fathers to sons within the companies
were regarded by insurers as more dependable than written standards
had been imposed on the companies by the town councils
questions.explanation: The phrase is set against a salaried department that ‘could be held to written standards of readiness’ and the author’s closing phrase ‘obligations that could be specified and enforced.’ Obligations of custom and honor are the contrast case: real, but unwritten and not formally enforceable. That is A. B is the tempting trap, but the author implies nothing about how seriously volunteers took their duties, only about how those duties could be enforced.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what “custom and honor” means in this contrast.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph: the “whereas” sentence and the paragraph’s final phrase.

breakdown.analysis: Look at the “whereas.” Paid department: answerable to a council, held to “written standards.” Volunteer company: obligations of “custom and honor.” The paragraph ends by praising obligations “that could be specified and enforced.” So custom and honor = not written down, not enforceable. Note what it doesn’t mean: it says nothing about volunteers being lazy.

choices.note: CORRECT. The contrast is written and enforceable vs. customary. Obligations resting on custom and honor have no formal mechanism to compel them.

Tempting, because unwritten duties sound weaker. But the author never says volunteers took their duties lightly; Brandt even found little evidence they fought fires worse. The point is enforceability, not effort.
Reads “custom” too literally. Nothing in the passage is about family inheritance.
Opposite. The insurers are suggested to have preferred written, enforceable standards.
Opposite. Council oversight is what the paid departments had; the volunteers’ obligations were a matter of custom.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Brandt’s account as it is described in the passage?
choices: Volunteer companies in Halvern frequently held public dinners to raise money for new equipment.
A few of the insurers that did business in Halvern charged the same premium regardless of the kind of fire department a town maintained.
Fire losses in Halvern’s towns declined in the years after paid departments were established.
The towns whose volunteer companies were disbanded earliest were, for the most part, the towns in which the large insurers began doing business latest.
Some members of disbanded volunteer companies later joined the paid departments that replaced them as salaried firefighters.
questions.explanation: The passage credits Brandt’s account with explaining the timing: disbanding followed the insurers’ arrival town by town. D says the earliest disbanding occurred where insurers arrived latest, which reverses that pattern and undercuts the causal story. C is the strongest trap: it might suggest paid departments were better, but it bears on what happened after the change, not on why the change was made, so it leaves Brandt’s explanation untouched. B concerns only a few insurers and so barely affects an account built on the large insurers’ rate schedules.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages Brandt’s insurance explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (her mechanism) and the third paragraph (the timing evidence).

breakdown.analysis: Brandt’s story is causal: insurers arrive, discounts for paid departments, so property owners vote out their own companies. Her best evidence is timing: disbanding followed the insurers’ arrival. So what if the timing ran the other way? A cause can’t come after its effect. We want an answer that breaks the insurer-then-disbanding sequence.

choices.note: Irrelevant. It shows volunteers cared about equipment, which, if anything, fits Brandt’s point that they kept pace.
Tempting but weak. “A few” insurers with flat rates don’t matter if the large insurers offered the discount, and Brandt’s mechanism runs through them.

Tempting. It sounds like paid departments were better, which echoes the standard view. But it’s about results after the switch, not about why towns switched. Brandt’s explanation of the cause survives.
CORRECT. Earliest disbanding where insurers arrived latest: the supposed cause shows up after the effect. That reverses the timing pattern Brandt relies on.
Irrelevant. Where the volunteers ended up doesn’t bear on why their companies were dissolved.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The Dolan test should be abandoned, and every identification obtained through an unnecessarily suggestive procedure should be excluded from trial.
Ferreira’s critique of the Dolan test fails, because a witness’s certainty remains a dependable guide to the accuracy of an identification.
Ferreira rightly shows that the Dolan test relies on measures that suggestion can distort, but that problem calls for a reformed test rather than wholesale exclusion.
Because suggestion can distort a witness’s memory, eyewitness identifications should never by themselves be sufficient to establish guilt.
Calvery’s courts have misapplied the Dolan test by giving too little weight to the witness’s opportunity to view the offender.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the Dolan test and Ferreira’s critique of it, then accepts her diagnosis (‘difficult to resist’) while arguing that her remedy of exclusion is broader than needed and that a reformed test would answer the problem, which is C. A is the trap: it is Ferreira’s conclusion, which the author resists except possibly for showups. B contradicts the author’s acceptance of her diagnosis.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one claim the whole passage builds toward.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentences of paragraphs 3 and 4 and the last sentence of the passage: ‘difficult to resist,’ ‘But her remedy sweeps more broadly,’ ‘a reformed test, not exclusion.’

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1 and 2 are setup: the rule and Ferreira’s attack on it. The author’s own view arrives in paragraph 3 (Ferreira’s diagnosis is right, her remedy goes too far) and paragraph 4 (here’s a better fix). So the main point has to carry both halves: yes to the diagnosis, no to blanket exclusion. Prephrase: Ferreira is right that the Dolan factors get contaminated, but the answer is a better test, not excluding everything.

choices.note: Tempting, but it’s Ferreira’s conclusion, not the author’s. The author says her remedy ‘sweeps more broadly than her diagnosis requires’ and proposes a reformed test instead. Don’t confuse a cited scholar’s view with the author’s.
Opposite. The author calls Ferreira’s diagnosis ‘difficult to resist’ and says certainty on the stand tells more about what happened to memory afterward than about the identification.
CORRECT. It captures both moves: the author accepts Ferreira’s diagnosis and rejects her blanket exclusion in favor of a reformed test (paragraphs 3 and 4).
Too broad and off topic. The passage is about how to treat suggestively obtained identifications, not whether any identification can be enough for a conviction.
Not stated. Nobody says courts misapply the test or underweight viewing opportunity. Ferreira’s complaint is that the factors themselves are contaminated.

questions.stem: In calling the Dolan test “a thermometer that the fever itself can reset” (second paragraph), Ferreira most probably means that
choices: the measures the test uses to detect harm from a suggestive procedure can themselves be altered by that procedure
the test yields results that vary unpredictably from one judge to another
judges’ own preconceptions about a defendant’s guilt distort how they apply the test
the reliability factors become less accurate simply because of the time that passes between the crime and the trial
the test can detect harm from a suggestive procedure only when the suggestion was mild
questions.explanation: The metaphor sums up the point just made in the second paragraph: a suggestive procedure inflates the witness’s certainty and recalled view and attention, which are the very factors the court uses to check whether the suggestion did harm, which is A. D is tempting because the author later mentions months passing, but Ferreira’s point is that the suggestion itself, not time alone, changes the measures. B and C bring in judges, who are not the source of the distortion she describes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decode the metaphor: what is the thermometer, what is the fever, and what does ‘reset’ mean?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, the two sentences before the phrase.

breakdown.analysis: Map it out. Thermometer = the Dolan reliability factors (certainty, view, attention), the tool used to check for harm. Fever = the suggestive procedure, the harm being checked for. Reset = confirming feedback inflates those very factors. So the thing being measured changes the measuring tool, and the worse the fever, the healthier the reading. It’s like letting a student grade the exam he cheated on. Prephrase: the suggestion corrupts the measures used to detect it.

choices.note: CORRECT. The suggestive procedure inflates the very factors the court uses to decide whether it did harm. That’s the fever resetting the thermometer.
Out of scope. Ferreira’s complaint isn’t inconsistency between judges. The test could be applied identically everywhere and still be corrupted.
Wrong source of distortion. In the metaphor, the fever is the suggestive procedure acting on the witness, not judges’ biases.

Tempting. The author does mention testimony ‘months after the procedure.’ But Ferreira’s point is specifically that the suggestion (confirming feedback) resets the measures. Time alone isn’t the fever.

Not supported. Ferreira’s point is the reverse: the worse the procedure, the more reliable the identification may look, so the test fails worst when suggestion is strong. Nothing says it works when suggestion is mild.

questions.stem: The author mentions a witness who recognizes a longtime neighbor as the offender (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that suggestive procedures are sometimes necessary for the police to identify an offender
illustrate how confirming feedback can inflate a witness’s confidence in an identification
provide an example of a case in which a court misapplied the factors listed in Dolan
suggest that witnesses who know the offender are not susceptible to errors of memory
give an instance in which excluding a suggestively obtained identification would discard evidence that is likely to be accurate
questions.explanation: The example follows the claim that Ferreira’s remedy ‘sweeps more broadly than her diagnosis requires’ and shows a case where exclusion would throw out a very likely accurate identification merely because a confirming remark followed it, which is E. D is the trap: the author calls such an identification ‘very likely accurate,’ not immune to memory error. B describes the second paragraph’s point, not this example.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author brings up the neighbor example.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, the sentence before the example (‘her remedy sweeps more broadly’) and the example itself.

breakdown.analysis: Look at the sentence right before: ‘her remedy sweeps more broadly than her diagnosis requires.’ The example backs that up. The witness already knows the neighbor and picked him from a fair lineup; the suggestive remark came only after her choice, so it can’t have produced it. Ferreira’s rule would still exclude it. Prephrase: it shows exclusion would throw out good evidence.

choices.note: Not the point. The author never says the confirming remark was necessary. The example is about what exclusion would cost, not why police used the procedure.

Tempting, because the example does include confirming feedback. But the author uses it to show what exclusion would cost, not how feedback inflates confidence; that mechanism is Ferreira’s point in paragraph 2.
No court decision is described. The example is hypothetical (‘for instance’) and is aimed at Ferreira’s remedy, not at a court.
Too strong. ‘Very likely accurate’ isn’t ‘immune to error.’ The author only needs this identification to be probably right for exclusion to look costly.
CORRECT. The example supports the claim that Ferreira’s remedy is too broad: blanket exclusion would sacrifice identifications that are very likely right.

questions.stem: According to the passage, under the rule announced in Regina v. Dolan, a judge who finds that an identification procedure was unnecessarily suggestive must
choices: exclude the resulting identification from trial
admit the identification if, considering all the circumstances, it appears reliable
instruct the jury to disregard the witness’s expressed certainty
require the police to conduct a new lineup that is not suggestive
admit the identification only if the witness had known the offender beforehand
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says a judge who finds a procedure unnecessarily suggestive ‘must nonetheless admit the identification if, considering all the circumstances, it appears reliable,’ which is B. A is what Ferreira proposes, not what Dolan requires.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the Dolan rule requires of the judge.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, the second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Straight detail. The Dolan rule: suggestive procedure does not mean automatic exclusion; the judge admits the identification if it looks reliable considering all the circumstances. Prephrase: admit it if it appears reliable.

choices.note: Wrong party. That’s Ferreira’s proposal in paragraph 2. Paragraph 1 says such identifications are ‘not automatically excluded.’
CORRECT. Paragraph 1 says this almost word for word.
Not stated. Certainty is one of the factors Dolan lists for the judge to consider, not something the jury is told to ignore.
Not stated. Nothing in the passage mentions ordering a new lineup.
Made up. Prior acquaintance comes up only in the author’s neighbor example, not in the Dolan rule.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Requiring police to record a witness’s initial confidence would remove the distorting effect of every kind of suggestive procedure.
Ferreira overstates the extent to which confirming feedback affects a witness’s later account of an identification.
Identifications obtained by showing a witness a single suspect should continue to be judged by the Dolan factors as courts now measure them.
A witness’s certainty at trial is a less trustworthy guide to accuracy than the witness’s confidence recorded at the first identification, before any feedback.
A witness’s opportunity to view the offender has no bearing on the reliability of the witness’s identification.
questions.explanation: In the third paragraph the author says certainty on the stand reflects what has happened to memory since the identification, and in the fourth proposes using confidence recorded at the first identification because it is fixed before feedback can act on it, so the author would agree with D. A is the main trap: the author concedes that such a record ‘would not cure every suggestive procedure,’ naming single-suspect showups. C fails because for showups the author says Ferreira’s strictness ‘may well be warranted.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the statement the author would endorse.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (certainty on the stand) and paragraph 4 (the recorded first-identification confidence and the ‘Admittedly’ concession).

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so collect the author’s commitments: 1. Ferreira’s diagnosis is right. 2. Certainty at trial mostly reflects what happened to memory after the identification. 3. Confidence recorded at the first identification is fixed before feedback, so courts should use it instead. 4. That fix doesn’t work for showups, where exclusion may be right. Put 2 and 3 together and the author plainly ranks the recorded initial confidence above trial certainty. Watch for answers that drop the ‘Admittedly’ concession.

choices.note: Tempting, but the author says the opposite: ‘such a record would not cure every suggestive procedure.’ A witness shown a single suspect is steered before any confidence can be stated. ‘Every’ is the giveaway.
The author calls Ferreira’s diagnosis ‘difficult to resist.’ Nowhere does the author doubt the effect of feedback.
Contradicts paragraph 4. For single-suspect procedures the author says ‘Ferreira’s strictness may well be warranted,’ which means exclusion, not the current test.

CORRECT. Trial certainty tells more about what happened to the memory afterward (paragraph 3), while the recorded initial confidence is fixed before feedback could act on it (paragraph 4). The author would rank the second as more trustworthy.
Too strong. Nobody says viewing opportunity is irrelevant. The problem is that witnesses’ later reports of their view can be inflated, not that the view itself doesn’t matter.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the author’s proposal in the fourth paragraph?
choices: Officers conducting lineups who know which person is the suspect often signal it unintentionally, through their manner, before the witness states any level of confidence.
Witnesses who receive confirming feedback after an identification often recall having had a better view of the offender than they reported beforehand.
Jurors tend to give great weight to the testimony of eyewitnesses who express certainty on the stand.
Recording a witness’s statement of confidence at the first identification takes little time and requires no special equipment.
In Calvery, police use single-suspect showups far less often than they use lineups.
questions.explanation: The proposal works only if confidence recorded at the first identification is free of suggestion because it comes before any feedback; A says suggestion commonly reaches the witness during ordinary lineups, before that confidence is stated, so the record would be contaminated too. B is tempting because it concerns distortion, but it describes the feedback effect the proposal is designed to get around, so it supports the proposal. E bears only on how often the author’s conceded exception arises.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages the author’s idea of using confidence recorded at the first identification.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially ‘before any feedback could be given’ and ‘fixed before the confirming remarks Ferreira describes could act on it.’

breakdown.analysis: The proposal assumes the suggestion comes after the choice (feedback), so a record made at the moment of choice is clean. The author admits one exception: showups, where suggestion acts before the choice. So ask: what if suggestion acts before the choice in ordinary lineups too? Then the ‘clean’ record isn’t clean, and the fix fails for the very procedures it was meant for. Prephrase: suggestion often reaches witnesses before they state their confidence, even in lineups.

choices.note: CORRECT. If officers commonly tip off witnesses during lineups, suggestion acts before the confidence is recorded, so the recorded confidence is contaminated too. That attacks the proposal’s key assumption and extends the author’s showup exception to ordinary lineups.

Tempting, since it’s about distortion. But this is the feedback effect from paragraph 2, which happens after the choice. The proposal is built to get around it, so this supports the need for the proposal.
If anything this strengthens the case for reform: if juries rely heavily on trial certainty, giving courts a cleaner measure matters more. It doesn’t show the proposal fails.
This makes the proposal easier to adopt. It strengthens, not weakens.
This only says the author’s conceded exception comes up less often. If anything, it makes the proposal cover more cases.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Tessel’s campion produces winged seeds chiefly to colonize newly opened ground, as botanists had long assumed, though the plants do so more in meadows than on slopes.
Ferrel’s experiments with light have shown that Aldane was mistaken in attributing the campion’s pattern of seed production to competition among relatives.
The proportion of winged seeds a campion plant produces is an inherited trait that differs between meadow and slope populations.
The campion’s greater production of winged seeds when crowded is well explained as reducing sibling competition, though the light cue that triggers it can mislead.
Plants that produce two kinds of seeds generally adjust the proportion of each in response to the quality of the light they receive.
questions.explanation: The passage explains Aldane’s puzzling finding with her kin-competition account, shows through experiments that the response is triggered by a red/far-red light cue, and ends by noting the cue can mislead, which is D. B is tempting because Ferrel’s work leads to a refinement, but the author says Aldane’s account ‘has held up well.’ C contradicts the greenhouse result, and E generalizes from one species to all plants with two kinds of seeds.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the whole passage supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (the puzzle), paragraph 2 (Aldane’s theory), and paragraph 5 (the author’s verdict).

breakdown.analysis: This is a puzzle-then-theory-then-mechanism passage. Puzzle: more winged seeds where dispersal seems least useful. Theory: Aldane’s kin competition. Mechanism: plants respond to crowding (Aldane) via a red/far-red cue (Ferrel). Twist: the cue sometimes misfires. A good main point names the explanation and acknowledges the refinement. Prephrase: Aldane’s kin-competition account explains the pattern, and the plants detect crowding through a light cue that isn’t foolproof.

choices.note: Contradicts the passage. Aldane’s survey made that old assumption ‘puzzling,’ and her explanation replaces it with kin competition.

Tempting. Ferrel’s work does lead to a refinement, but it explains how the plants sense crowding; it doesn’t overturn the kin-competition explanation. The author says Aldane’s account ‘has held up well.’
Contradicts paragraph 3: the difference ‘was not inherited but a response to the conditions each plant encountered.’
CORRECT. It covers the explanation (sibling competition), the mechanism (a light cue), and the reservation (the cue can mislead), in the passage’s measured tone.
Too broad. The passage is about one species. Nothing says all plants with two seed types respond to light this way.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Aldane’s greenhouse experiment showed that
choices: plants whose parents came from meadows produced a higher proportion of winged seeds than plants whose parents came from slopes, at either density
the proportion of winged seeds a plant produced depended on the density at which it was grown rather than on the habitat from which its parent came
a low ratio of red to far-red light was by itself sufficient to raise the proportion of winged seeds a plant produced
plants grown at high density produced fewer seeds in total than plants grown at low density
the proportion of winged seeds a plant produced depended both on the density at which it was grown and on the habitat from which its parent came
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says crowded plants produced a high proportion of winged seeds and sparse plants a low one ‘regardless of whether their parents had come from meadow or slope,’ which is B. C is the trap: it is true according to the passage, but it was Ferrel’s 2010 finding, not Aldane’s. E and A contradict ‘regardless.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Aldane’s greenhouse experiment showed.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, the second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Aldane grew seedlings from both habitats at high and low density. Result: density predicted the proportion of winged seeds; parent’s habitat didn’t. Prephrase: density, not origin, determined the proportion. On detail questions, check who did what. This passage has two researchers.

choices.note: Contradicts ‘regardless of whether their parents had come from meadow or slope.’ Origin made no difference.
CORRECT. Paragraph 3 says exactly this: crowded plants made more winged seeds, sparse plants fewer, regardless of parent habitat.
Tempting. It’s true, but it’s Ferrel’s finding (paragraph 4), from a different experiment with adjustable lamps. Wrong party.
Not stated. The passage talks about proportions of winged seeds, never total seed counts.
Half right. Density mattered, but the parent’s habitat didn’t: ‘regardless’ rules out the ‘both’.

questions.stem: The author discusses a parent that drops forty heavy seeds where two gaps open (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: estimate the number of gaps that typically open around a campion plant in a valley meadow in a single season
show that heavy seeds are less likely than winged seeds to germinate once they reach a gap in the turf
explain why plants on disturbed slopes produce fewer seeds in total than plants in meadows
suggest that winged seeds seldom travel far enough to escape competition with their siblings
illustrate why, in crowded conditions, adding seeds beside the parent does little to increase the parent’s descendants
questions.explanation: The forty-seeds example is a worked illustration of Aldane’s logic: only as many seeds as there are gaps can establish nearby, so extra heavy seeds are simply lost, which is E. A is tempting because the example uses numbers, but it begins with ‘Suppose’ and is hypothetical, not an estimate. D reverses the point: winged seeds are said to escape sibling competition.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author includes the forty-seeds, two-gaps example.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, the third sentence (‘Suppose...’) and the sentences on either side.

breakdown.analysis: So what does the example do? It makes Aldane’s idea concrete. Two gaps, forty seeds: two can make it, thirty-eight are wasted, and dropping a forty-first changes nothing. That’s why the next sentence turns to winged seeds, which can fill gaps elsewhere. Prephrase: it illustrates why piling more seeds next to the parent is wasted when space nearby is limited.

choices.note: Tempting, but ‘Suppose’ marks a hypothetical. The numbers are made up to show a principle, not to report or estimate actual gap counts.
Not the point. Germination rates of the two seed types are never compared. The issue is competition for a fixed number of gaps, not which seed sprouts better.
Wrong comparison. The example is about a meadow, and total seed production is never discussed.
Reversed. The passage says a winged seed ‘competes mostly with the offspring of other plants,’ that is, it does escape siblings.
CORRECT. Only as many nearby seeds can establish as there are gaps, so extra heavy seeds add nothing. That’s the logic of Aldane’s kin-competition explanation.

questions.stem: In saying that on a disturbed slope “the arithmetic is different” (end of the second paragraph), the author most likely means that on such a slope
choices: plants produce fewer seeds in total, so fewer of their seeds are lost to competition
winged seeds carried away from the parent compete mostly with the offspring of other plants
heavy seeds that fall near the parent are likely to find room to establish rather than merely displacing siblings
the number of gaps that open in a season cannot be predicted from the density of the surrounding plants
a parent gains more descendants from each winged seed than from each heavy seed
questions.explanation: The ‘arithmetic’ refers to the forty-seeds, two-gaps calculation; on a slope, open ground near the parent is plentiful, so heavy seeds dropped nearby are seldom wasted, which is C. B is tempting because it uses the passage’s words, but that is true of winged seeds in meadows too, so it isn’t what’s different about slopes. E describes the meadow situation, the opposite of the slope.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decode ‘the arithmetic is different’: different from what, and how?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2: the forty-seeds calculation and the sentence that contains the phrase.

breakdown.analysis: ‘The arithmetic’ points back to the forty-seeds example: in a meadow, few gaps means most nearby seeds are wasted. On a slope, the author explains right after the colon: open ground near the parent is plentiful and the site is proven suitable, so nearby heavy seeds ‘are seldom wasted.’ Prephrase: on slopes, nearby heavy seeds have room to grow, so they aren’t wasted the way they are in meadows.

choices.note: Not stated. The passage compares proportions of seed types, not total seed output. And the reason given for the difference is plentiful open ground, not fewer seeds.
Tempting. This is from the passage, but it describes winged seeds generally and is true in meadows as well. It doesn’t say what’s different about slopes.
CORRECT. With plentiful open ground nearby, heavy seeds can establish instead of crowding out siblings. That’s why the calculation comes out differently.
Not the point. The author isn’t saying gap numbers are unpredictable on slopes; she says gaps there are plentiful.
Opposite. On slopes, heavy seeds are seldom wasted, which is why slope plants make only about 15 percent winged seeds. A winged seed being worth more is the meadow situation.

questions.stem: The information in the passage most strongly supports which one of the following about the plants grown at high density in Aldane’s greenhouse experiment?
choices: The light reaching them was probably poorer in red relative to far-red than the light reaching the plants grown at low density.
They produced a high proportion of winged seeds because their neighbors reduced the overall intensity of the light reaching them.
They produced more winged seeds in absolute number than did the plants grown at low density.
Those whose parents came from slopes produced a lower proportion of winged seeds than did those whose parents came from meadows.
Their winged seeds would have been less likely to reach gaps than the winged seeds of the plants grown at low density.
questions.explanation: Combining the third and fourth paragraphs: crowded plants made more winged seeds, and Ferrel showed the plants sense crowding through light that has passed through or bounced off neighbors’ leaves, which is poor in red relative to far-red, so A is strongly supported. B is the main trap: Ferrel found that dimming the light without changing the ratio had no effect, so overall intensity isn’t the trigger. C confuses a proportion with an absolute number.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer something about the crowded plants in Aldane’s greenhouse.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (the experiment) combined with paragraph 4 (Ferrel’s light mechanism).

breakdown.analysis: This one requires connecting two paragraphs. Paragraph 3: crowded plants → high proportion of winged seeds. Paragraph 4: how plants sense crowding → neighbors’ leaves absorb red and pass on far-red, so the light is poor in red; a low red/far-red ratio alone raises winged-seed proportion; dimming alone does nothing. Put together: the crowded pots were most likely getting low-ratio light from neighbors. Prephrase: the crowded plants were probably getting light with a low red-to-far-red ratio.

choices.note: CORRECT. Crowded plants are surrounded by neighbors’ foliage, which makes the light relatively poor in red. Ferrel’s work identifies that as the cue that raises the winged-seed proportion. ‘Probably’ keeps this at the right strength.
Tempting. Neighbors do shade each other, so it sounds natural. But Ferrel found that ‘merely dimming the lamps had no effect.’ Intensity isn’t the trigger; the ratio is.
Proportion isn’t number. Crowded plants had a higher share of winged seeds, but they could have produced fewer seeds overall. Know this trap: a percentage tells you nothing about the total.
Contradicts ‘regardless of whether their parents had come from meadow or slope.’
Unsupported. The experiment measured how many winged seeds were produced, not where they landed. Nothing suggests density affects how far a winged seed travels.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the author’s suggestion that the seed allocation of campion growing beneath birch may serve those plants poorly?
choices: Beneath young birch stands, the ratio of red to far-red light is as low as it is in the densest valley-floor meadows.
Campion growing beneath birch produce fewer seeds in total than campion growing in the open on the same slopes.
Winged seeds produced by meadow plants are more likely to reach a gap than are winged seeds produced by birch-shaded plants.
Seedlings that establish beneath young birch stands seldom survive to flower, because the shade deepens as the trees mature.
Campion from open slopes that are grown under light filtered through birch leaves produce winged seeds in meadow proportions.
questions.explanation: The author suspects the birch-shaded plants waste effort on winged seeds because the open ground beneath them would let heavy seeds establish nearby. D shows that seedlings near the parent seldom survive to flower anyway, so dispersing seeds away is actually the better strategy there, and the allocation may serve the plants well. A and E are the tempting traps: they confirm that the birch light triggers the response, which explains the behavior but says nothing about whether it helps or hurts the plant. B concerns total output, not allocation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that makes it less likely that heavy winged-seed production hurts birch-shaded plants.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4 (the birch case) and paragraph 5 (‘may serve it poorly’), with the logic of paragraph 2.

breakdown.analysis: Why does the author think the birch plants are making a mistake? Because the logic of paragraph 2 says winged seeds pay off when nearby ground is crowded, and under birch ‘the ground below is open and gaps are plentiful.’ So heavy seeds should do fine there, and the extra winged seeds look wasteful. To call that into question, show that heavy seeds dropped near the parent won’t do fine after all, even with open ground. Prephrase: something makes the spot near the parent bad for offspring, so sending seeds away is smart. Expect the right answer to look sideways; the traps will be about the light cue.

choices.note: Tempting. This explains why birch-shaded plants make so many winged seeds. But explaining the cause of a behavior doesn’t tell you whether the behavior helps the plant. The question is about results, not mechanism.
Irrelevant. Total seed output isn’t the issue. The question is whether the split between winged and heavy seeds is a bad one.
If anything this supports the author: if birch plants’ winged seeds are less likely to find gaps, investing in them looks even worse. It certainly doesn’t call the suggestion into question.

CORRECT. The suggestion rests on the idea that nearby heavy seeds would succeed under birch because gaps are plentiful. If seedlings there rarely survive to flower, nearby seeds are wasted after all, and sending seeds away on wings is the better bet. The ‘mistake’ might actually be a good strategy.
Tempting. This confirms that birch-filtered light triggers the meadow response. But that’s already what the author assumes. Confirming the mechanism does nothing to show the response pays off.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Aldane’s explanation of the campion’s seed production can most accurately be described as
choices: skeptical, because Aldane’s greenhouse experiment could not distinguish inherited differences from responses to the conditions a plant encountered
largely approving, while suggesting that the plants respond to a correlate of crowding rather than to crowding itself
neutral, since the author reports Aldane’s findings and Ferrel’s without evaluating either
dismissive, because Ferrel’s later work showed that light quality, not competition, governs the plants’ seed production
wholly approving, since later work has confirmed every element of the explanation
questions.explanation: In the last paragraph the author says Aldane’s account ‘has held up well’ but needs a refinement: the plant responds to a signal that usually accompanies crowding rather than to crowding itself, which is B. E is too strong, since the author proposes a refinement and notes that the cue can mislead. D confuses the trigger (light) with the reason the response exists (competition), which Ferrel’s work doesn’t displace.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the attitude, with its reason, that matches how the author views Aldane’s explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 5, the first sentence, plus paragraph 3 (‘Aldane’s account implied that the plants could detect crowding’).

breakdown.analysis: The author’s verdict is spelled out: ‘Aldane’s account has held up well, but such cases suggest a refinement of it.’ The refinement: plants don’t detect crowding itself (as Aldane’s account implied) but a light signal that usually goes with it. So: positive overall, with one qualification. That’s the classic LSAT author: favorable with a reservation. Prephrase: approving, with a refinement about what the plants actually sense.

choices.note: Wrong on the facts. The greenhouse experiment is exactly what separated inheritance from response: proportions tracked density ‘regardless’ of parent habitat. And the author isn’t skeptical overall.
CORRECT. ‘Held up well’ is approval; the refinement is that the campion responds ‘not to crowding itself but to a signal that ordinarily accompanies crowding.’
The author does evaluate: ‘has held up well,’ ‘the cue is imperfect,’ ‘may serve it poorly.’ That’s not neutral.

Tempting if you mix up the trigger and the purpose. Ferrel showed light is how plants detect crowding; the reason for responding to crowding is still competition among relatives. The author keeps Aldane’s account.
Too strong. The author proposes a refinement and points to cases where the plants’ response may misfire. ‘Every element’ ignores that.

questions.stimulus: Dog owner: Veterinarians routinely urge owners to have their dogs' teeth professionally cleaned every year to prevent gum disease. But my terrier, Biscuit, lived to the age of fifteen without a single cleaning, and his gums stayed healthy to the end. Clearly, the risk that gum disease poses to dogs whose teeth are never cleaned has been greatly exaggerated.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the dog owner's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: attacks the motives of veterinarians rather than addressing the evidence for their recommendation
presumes, without providing justification, that annual cleanings are the only way to prevent gum disease
draws a general conclusion from a single case that may not be typical
fails to consider that some dogs whose teeth are cleaned every year still develop gum disease
takes for granted that a recommendation made by most experts must be correct
questions.explanation: One healthy terrier tells us almost nothing about how often uncleaned teeth lead to gum disease in dogs generally, so C names the flaw. A is tempting because the owner is disagreeing with veterinarians, but the owner never questions their motives; the problem is the evidence, not an attack on the source.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The risk of gum disease for dogs whose teeth are never cleaned has been greatly exaggerated.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Biscuit never had a cleaning and his gums stayed healthy for fifteen years.

breakdown.analysis: So what if Biscuit was fine? One dog is one dog. Structure: 1. Vets say annual cleanings prevent gum disease. 2. Biscuit had no cleanings and no gum disease. So the risk is exaggerated. That's the anecdote-versus-general-claim flaw; it's a classic, know it. It's like saying: my uncle smoked and lived to 90, so the risks of smoking are exaggerated. We need an answer that says the owner generalizes from one possibly lucky case.

choices.note: Tempting, because the owner is pushing back on veterinarians. But the owner never says vets have bad motives (like wanting to sell cleanings). No attack on motives happens here.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Vets only recommend yearly cleanings because they get paid for them, so we can ignore the advice.

choices.note: The owner never claims cleanings are the only prevention. The owner claims the risk without cleanings is small. Different claim.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Since Biscuit wasn't cleaned, he must have gotten gum disease, because cleaning is the only way to prevent it.

choices.note: CORRECT. The whole argument rests on one dog. Biscuit might have had unusually good genes or diet. A single case can't show what usually happens to dogs.
Irrelevant. If cleaned dogs sometimes get gum disease anyway, that would, if anything, help the owner. It isn't something the argument needed to consider.
choices.example: Example of a real failure to consider: Cleaned dogs rarely get gum disease, so cleaning prevents it (ignoring that owners who pay for cleanings may also feed better diets).

choices.note: Backwards. The owner rejects the experts' recommendation; he certainly doesn't assume they must be right.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most vets recommend yearly cleanings, so yearly cleanings must be necessary.

questions.stimulus: Railway manager: Last year we installed digital displays on the platforms at Hollin Junction that show exactly how many minutes remain until each train arrives. Since then, complaints from Hollin Junction passengers about delays have fallen by half, even though trains there have run late just as often as before. So the displays, by telling passengers what to expect, have made delays less frustrating for them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the railway manager's argument?
choices: At the railway's other stations, which did not receive displays, complaints about delays did not decline over the same period.
Passengers at Hollin Junction complain more often about crowded trains than about late trains.
The displays at Hollin Junction cost less to install than the railway had originally projected.
Some passengers at Hollin Junction say that they rarely look at the platform displays.
Trains at Hollin Junction are, on average, late by fewer minutes than trains at most of the railway's other stations.
