questions.explanation: The manager credits the displays for the drop in complaints, so an answer that rules out a railway-wide cause helps; A shows that stations without displays saw no such drop. E is tempting because it is about lateness, but it compares Hollin with other stations at one time and says nothing about why complaints at Hollin changed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The displays made delays less frustrating for Hollin Junction passengers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the displays went up, delay complaints at Hollin fell by half; trains ran late as often as before.

breakdown.analysis: Complaints dropped after the displays went in. But was it the displays? Maybe complaints dropped everywhere, say because the railway made complaining harder or delays got shorter systemwide. To strengthen a before-and-after causal claim, rule out other causes. We need an answer that says complaints didn't fall at places without displays.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the comparison group. Stations without displays saw no drop, so a systemwide cause is less likely and the displays look like the difference.
Wrong topic. Crowding complaints don't tell us why delay complaints fell.
Wrong dimension. Installation cost has nothing to do with whether the displays reduced frustration.
This slightly weakens the argument: displays nobody looks at can't calm anybody. Wrong direction.
Tempting, since it's about lateness. But it's a snapshot comparison between stations. The argument is about a change at Hollin over time, and we already know Hollin's lateness didn't change.

questions.stimulus:
Marisol: The city arts council should stop giving grants to the Brindle Street Theater. Its productions sell out every night, so its ticket sales obviously cover its costs, and grant money should go to companies that cannot pay their own way.

Teodor: Selling out every night does not mean the Brindle covers its costs. Its auditorium holds only ninety seats, and it deliberately keeps its ticket prices low. Without the grant, it would have to raise its prices sharply, and many of the people who now attend could no longer afford to.
questions.stem: Marisol and Teodor disagree over whether
choices: grant money should go to theater companies that cannot pay their own way
the Brindle Street Theater's productions are popular with audiences
a theater company that receives a grant should keep its ticket prices low
the Brindle Street Theater's ticket sales cover its costs
the arts council's grants are responsible for the Brindle Street Theater's sold-out shows
questions.explanation: Marisol says the sold-out shows mean ticket sales obviously cover the Brindle's costs; Teodor flatly denies that, so D is the point at issue. C is tempting because Teodor values low prices, but Marisol says nothing about ticket prices, so there is no disagreement there.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Marisol: The Brindle sells out, so its ticket sales cover its costs; grants should go to companies that can't pay their way. Teodor: Selling out doesn't mean it covers its costs; with only ninety seats and low prices, it needs the grant.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Marisol: ticket sales cover costs, yes. Teodor's first sentence: no, they don't. That's the clash. Notice what Teodor doesn't attack: Marisol's principle that grants should go to companies that can't pay their way. He may well accept it; he just thinks the Brindle is one of those companies.

choices.note: Tempting, but Teodor never rejects this principle. His point is that the Brindle can't pay its way, which fits the principle. No disagreement.
Both agree. Marisol says it sells out every night; Teodor accepts that and argues from it.
Tempting, since Teodor cares about keeping prices low. But Marisol says nothing about ticket prices. One speaker silent means no disagreement we can confirm.
CORRECT. Marisol: yes, ticket sales obviously cover its costs. Teodor: selling out does not mean it covers its costs. Direct yes/no.
Neither speaker says the grants cause the sell-outs. Teodor's point is about prices and costs, not about why shows sell out.

questions.stimulus: Restorers at the Vell Gallery who remove old varnish from paintings have noticed something surprising. Yellowed varnish is generally regarded as a defect, since it dulls a painting's colors. Yet the paint beneath the most heavily yellowed varnish is usually in better condition than the paint beneath varnish that has stayed clear.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the restorers' observation?
choices: Removing heavily yellowed varnish is a slow process that requires highly trained restorers.
The chemical change that makes varnish turn yellow also makes it better at blocking the light that fades and cracks paint.
Some of the paintings in the Vell Gallery's collection were never varnished at all.
Visitors to the gallery generally prefer to view paintings from which yellowed varnish has been removed.
Varnish yellows more quickly in damp conditions, which are also harmful to the paint beneath it.
questions.explanation: The puzzle is why a supposed defect goes with healthier paint; B explains it by showing that the yellowing itself protects the paint from damaging light. E is the trap: it ties yellowing to damp, which harms paint, so it makes the observation more puzzling rather than less.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Yellowed varnish is considered a defect, but paint under the most yellowed varnish tends to be in the best shape.

breakdown.analysis: How can a defect go along with better paint? Classic paradox engine: the defect turns out to help. Yellowing is bad for how a painting looks, but that doesn't mean it's bad for the paint. We need an answer that shows yellow varnish somehow protects what's underneath.

choices.note: So? How hard yellow varnish is to remove says nothing about why the paint under it is healthier.
CORRECT. The same change that dulls the colors shields the paint from light damage. A defect in looks, a benefit for preservation. Both facts now fit.
Irrelevant. Unvarnished paintings aren't part of the comparison between yellowed and clear varnish.
Visitor taste is the wrong dimension. It doesn't explain the physical condition of the paint.
Opposite direction. If yellowing goes with damp, and damp harms paint, we'd expect worse paint under yellow varnish. This deepens the puzzle.

questions.stimulus: Campaign manager: Only about 12 percent of Dunmere's registered voters cast ballots in last May's election for the town water board, whereas more than 60 percent voted in last November's election for mayor. So if the water-board election were moved to November and placed on the same ballot as the mayor's race, far more voters would help choose the water board's members.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the campaign manager's argument?
choices: Most voters who take part in November elections are well informed about the water board's responsibilities.
Turnout in Dunmere's November elections will be at least as high in future years as it was last year.
Everyone who voted in last May's water-board election would also vote in a November election.
Moving the water-board election to November would not increase the cost of running Dunmere's elections.
A substantial number of the voters who cast ballots in November would not leave the water-board race blank.
questions.explanation: Showing up to vote is not the same as voting in every race on the ballot; the argument needs E, that many November voters would actually mark a choice for water board. Negate E (nearly all leave it blank) and the plan adds no voters. B is the too-strong trap: turnout could dip a little from 60 percent and still dwarf 12 percent.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Moving the water-board race to the November ballot would mean far more voters help choose the board.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: May water-board turnout was about 12 percent; November mayoral turnout was over 60 percent.

breakdown.analysis: More people would hold the ballot. But would they vote in the water-board race? People who come out for mayor might skip the obscure races further down. The argument quietly treats 'cast a ballot' as 'voted in every race'. We need an answer that says enough November voters would actually fill in the water-board line.

choices.note: Not required. Voters don't have to be well informed to cast a vote. Negated, the argument still stands.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most November voters are well informed about the water board. (They can still vote in the race.)

choices.note: Tempting, but too strong. Turnout could fall to 50 percent and still crush 12 percent. The argument survives the negation.
choices.negation: Turnout in future November elections will be somewhat lower than last year's. (Still far above 12 percent.)

choices.note: Too strong. If a few May voters skipped November, the total could still rise enormously.
choices.negation: At least one person who voted in May would not vote in November. (Doesn't matter given the size of the gap.)

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The conclusion is about how many people vote, not about cost.
choices.negation: Moving the election would increase the cost of running elections. (More voters could still take part.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it and almost every November voter leaves the water-board race blank. Then turnout for the ballot rises but participation in the water-board choice doesn't. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: Almost none of the November voters would mark a choice in the water-board race.

questions.stimulus: In a psychology study, volunteers memorized a list of words in either a quiet room or a room filled with recorded café noise. Later, each volunteer was tested on the list in either the same kind of room or the other kind. Volunteers tested in the same kind of room in which they had memorized the list recalled more words, on average, than those tested in the other kind of room. This held both for volunteers who memorized in the quiet room and for those who memorized in the noisy one.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Background noise interferes with memorizing words more than quiet does.
How closely the setting of recall matches the setting of learning can affect how much is recalled.
People who study in noisy places generally remember less of what they study than people who study in quiet places.
Volunteers who memorized the list in quiet and were tested in noise recalled more words than those who both memorized and were tested in noise.
How much a person recalls is unaffected by the noise level of the room in which the person is tested.
questions.explanation: In both groups, matching the test room to the learning room raised recall, which directly supports B. A and C are the tempting traps: they claim noise itself is worse, but the study never compares quiet learners with noisy learners overall, and noisy learners did better in a noisy test room.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Volunteers memorized words in a quiet or noisy room; 2. they were tested in the same kind of room or the other kind; 3. same-room testers recalled more on average; 4. this was true for quiet learners and noisy learners alike.

breakdown.analysis: The pattern is all about the match. Quiet learners did best in quiet; noisy learners did best in noise. Nothing here says quiet or noise is better in itself. Watch for answers that sneak in 'noise is bad'. We want the modest claim that matching settings matters.

choices.note: Tempting, because we assume noise is distracting. But the study never compares how much quiet learners and noisy learners recalled overall. Unsupported.
CORRECT. Matching rooms raised recall for both groups. 'Can affect' is modest, and the data back it fully.
Same trap as A, now stretched to people in general. The study shows noisy learners did better when tested in noise, not that they remember less overall.
We don't know this. The study reports same-room versus other-room averages, not this specific cross comparison.
Contradicted. For quiet learners, testing in noise lowered recall, so the test room's noise level did make a difference.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Two years ago, the province of Arlen cut its tax on gasoline by ten cents a liter. Since then, the number of cars registered in Arlen has risen by 8 percent. Evidently, the tax cut encouraged Arlen's residents to buy more cars.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the economist's argument?
choices: After the tax cut, the price of gasoline at Arlen's filling stations fell by nearly the full amount of the cut.
Some residents of Arlen who bought cars in the past two years did so for reasons unrelated to fuel costs.
Arlen's gasoline tax, even after the cut, is higher than the gasoline taxes of most neighboring provinces.
Over the same two years, car registrations rose by about as much in neighboring provinces whose gasoline taxes did not change.
The revenue Arlen lost because of the tax cut was made up by an increase in the province's sales tax.
questions.explanation: If registrations rose just as much in neighboring provinces with no tax cut, something other than the cut is probably driving car buying, which is what D shows. B is tempting, but 'some' buyers having other reasons is fully compatible with the cut prompting many others.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The gasoline tax cut encouraged Arlen residents to buy more cars.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the tax cut, car registrations in Arlen rose 8 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Registrations went up after the cut. But maybe they'd have gone up anyway: a growing economy, a growing population, a regional trend. Before-and-after is not cause. We need an answer that shows the rise happened without a tax cut too.

choices.note: This helps the economist: the cut really did make gas cheaper, which is how it would encourage car buying. Wrong direction.
Tempting, but 'some' is far too weak. Of course a few buyers had other reasons. The cut could still explain the overall rise.
So? Comparing tax levels across provinces doesn't tell us whether Arlen's cut changed behavior inside Arlen.
CORRECT. The comparison group. Provinces with no cut saw the same rise, so the rise in Arlen likely has some regional cause, not the tax cut.

Irrelevant. How the province replaced the revenue doesn't show whether the cut affected car buying. It's merely possible a sales tax rise discouraged purchases, and that would only make the 8 percent rise more impressive.

questions.stimulus: Conservator: Many museums now remove the overpaint that earlier restorers added to old paintings, on the grounds that it is not the original artist's work. Yet some overpaint is itself centuries old and records how later generations understood the painting. Removing it destroys historical evidence that can never be recovered. So, although overpaint that hides or harms original paint may need to come off, a museum should not remove old overpaint merely because the original artist did not apply it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the conservator's argument?
choices: Old overpaint should not be removed from a painting merely because the original artist did not apply it.
Removing overpaint from old paintings destroys historical evidence that can never be recovered.
Overpaint that hides or harms a painting's original paint should be removed.
Many museums now remove the overpaint that earlier restorers added to old paintings.
Some overpaint records how later generations understood the paintings to which it was added.
questions.explanation: Everything builds to the last clause: old overpaint should not be removed merely because the artist didn't apply it, which A restates. B is the tempting trap; it is a premise supporting that conclusion, and C is only the conservator's concession.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A museum should not remove old overpaint merely because the original artist didn't apply it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some overpaint is centuries old and records later understanding; removing it destroys unrecoverable evidence.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Sentence 1 is background (what museums do and why). Sentences 2 and 3 are reasons. The last sentence opens with a concession ('although ... may need to come off') and then gives the claim the reasons were for. That final 'should not remove ... merely because' is the conclusion.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the final claim, minus the concession: old overpaint shouldn't come off just because someone other than the artist applied it.
Tempting, because it's the strongest-sounding claim. But it's a reason given for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself. Ask: does this support the 'should not' claim? Yes. So it's a premise.
This is the concession. The conservator grants it ('may need to come off') but it isn't what the argument is trying to prove. Also, 'should be removed' is stronger than 'may need to.'
Background. It sets up the view the conservator is responding to.
A premise. It supports the claim that removal destroys evidence.

questions.stimulus: Psychologist: In a recent study, people who described themselves as habitual procrastinators kept a daily diary for a month. On 70 percent of the days on which they put off an important task, they reported feeling anxious that evening. This shows that putting off important tasks tends to make habitual procrastinators anxious.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the psychologist's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: draws a conclusion about people in general from a study limited to habitual procrastinators
takes for granted that the participants put off unimportant tasks less often than important ones
confuses a condition that is necessary for feeling anxious with one that is sufficient for it
presumes, without providing justification, that the participants were right to describe themselves as habitual procrastinators
fails to consider how often the participants felt anxious on days on which they did not put off an important task
questions.explanation: Seventy percent means nothing without a baseline: if the participants felt anxious on 70 percent of all their evenings, procrastinating made no difference, so E names the missing comparison. A is tempting but misreads the conclusion, which is limited to habitual procrastinators, the very group studied.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Putting off important tasks tends to make habitual procrastinators anxious.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: On 70 percent of the days they put off an important task, participants reported anxiety that evening.

breakdown.analysis: Seventy percent sounds high. High compared to what? If these people feel anxious on 70 percent of all evenings, procrastination changes nothing. This is the missing comparison group: the study reports what happened on procrastination days only. It's like saying a lucky sweater works because your team won 70 percent of the games you wore it, without checking how often they win when you don't. We need an answer that points to the non-procrastination days.

choices.note: Tempting at a glance, but read the conclusion: it's about habitual procrastinators only, the same group studied. No leap to people in general.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Habitual procrastinators get anxious when they delay tasks, so everyone does.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Unimportant tasks never enter the argument, and nothing depends on how often they're delayed.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Since procrastinators delay important tasks, they must delay trivial ones even more.

choices.note: No conditional confusion here. The psychologist never treats procrastination as required for anxiety or as guaranteeing it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Anyone who procrastinates gets anxious, so anyone anxious must have procrastinated.

choices.note: So? If a few participants weren't 'true' procrastinators, the core problem remains. This is a nitpick about labels, not the gap.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our survey respondents call themselves early risers, so they must wake before six.

choices.note: CORRECT. Without the anxiety rate on other days, 70 percent has no baseline. If they're anxious 70 percent of the time anyway, procrastinating makes no difference.

questions.stimulus: Veterinarian: The Tulls' elderly cat has a tumor that could be surgically removed. But the cat would face several weeks of painful recovery, and even with the surgery it would probably live only a few months longer than it would without it. So although the Tulls could easily afford the operation, I advised them against it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the veterinarian's reasoning?
choices: A veterinarian should advise against any treatment that the animal's owners would not be able to afford easily.
Whether an animal undergoes surgery should be decided by its owners rather than by its veterinarian.
A veterinarian should advise against surgery that would bring a painful recovery and likely add only a few months of life.
A veterinarian should recommend surgery whenever it is likely to extend an animal's life.
A veterinarian should advise against surgery for an animal only if the animal is unlikely to survive the operation.
questions.explanation: The vet's reasons are a painful recovery and only a few extra months of life, and C says exactly those two facts call for advising against surgery. E is tempting because it is about when to advise against surgery, but it would forbid this advice, since nothing suggests the cat would not survive the operation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The veterinarian was right to advise the Tulls against the surgery.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Recovery would be painful for weeks; the surgery would probably add only a few months of life; cost is not an issue.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, using the facts you're given. The facts: painful recovery, little extra life, money no problem. The action: advise against surgery. We need a rule like: if recovery is painful and the gain in life is small, advise against.

choices.note: Wrong facts. The Tulls can easily afford it, so this rule doesn't apply and gives no support.
Doesn't justify the advice. Owners deciding is consistent with a vet giving advice either way.
CORRECT. Both conditions match: painful recovery, and no more than a few months gained. The rule then says advise against, which is what the vet did.
Opposite. Surgery would extend life a little, so this rule would call for recommending it.
Tempting, since it's about advising against surgery. But 'only if' makes survival risk a requirement, and nothing says the cat might not survive. So this rule would actually condemn the advice.

questions.stimulus: Marine biologist: The striped blenny, a small reef fish, often bobs its head rapidly when another blenny approaches. Male blennies do this far more often than females do, and only males defend territories on the reef. So the head-bobbing is probably a warning that a male uses to drive rivals away from his territory.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the marine biologist's argument?
choices: Male blennies that lose their territories stop bobbing their heads within a few days.
Male blennies bob their heads far more often when a female approaches than when another male does.
Several other reef fish species defend territories without making any head movements.
Head-bobbing is common among many species of small reef fish.
Blennies bob their heads more rapidly in warm water than in cool water.
questions.explanation: If males bob mostly at approaching females, the display looks like courtship rather than a warning to rivals, so B undercuts the proposed function. A is tempting because it ties bobbing to territory, but that link supports the biologist's view rather than weakening it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Head-bobbing is probably a male's warning to drive rivals from his territory.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Blennies bob when another approaches; males bob far more than females; only males hold territories.

breakdown.analysis: The biologist guesses a function from who does it. But males do lots of things females don't, like courting. Maybe the bob is about attracting mates, not repelling rivals. When an argument guesses what a trait is for, weaken it with a different job the trait could be doing. We need an answer that points to another function, ideally tied to who the bob is aimed at.

choices.note: Tempting, since it mentions territory. But it strengthens the biologist: no territory, no bobbing, which fits a territorial warning. Wrong direction.
CORRECT. If males bob mostly at females, the bob looks like a courtship signal. A warning to rivals should be aimed at rival males.
So? Other species defending territories some other way says nothing about what this blenny's bob is for.
Irrelevant. That many fish bob doesn't tell us what blennies bob for.
Irrelevant. Water temperature affecting speed says nothing about the bob's purpose.

questions.stimulus: Councilor: Some residents propose that only people who have lived in Fairhaven for at least ten years be allowed to serve on its planning commission, on the grounds that long residence ensures familiarity with the town's needs. But under that rule, the engineer who designed Fairhaven's flood-control system, who moved here six years ago and knows the town's drainage better than anyone, would be barred from serving. Clearly, length of residence is a poor test of familiarity with the town's needs.
questions.stem: The claim that the engineer who designed Fairhaven's flood-control system would be barred from serving plays which one of the following roles in the councilor's argument?
choices: It is the conclusion that the councilor's argument is designed to establish.
It is a premise offered in support of the residents' proposal.
It is a general principle from which the councilor's conclusion is derived.
It is offered as evidence that the residents' proposal would be difficult to enforce.
It is presented as an unacceptable result of adopting the criterion that the residents propose.
questions.explanation: The councilor shows that the ten-year rule would exclude the person who arguably knows the town's needs best and uses that bad result to reject the rule's premise, so E is right. D is tempting because the claim is aimed against the proposal, but the councilor's point is that the rule gives the wrong answer, not that it is hard to enforce.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Length of residence is a poor test of familiarity with Fairhaven's needs.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Under the ten-year rule, the flood-control engineer, who knows the town's drainage best, would be barred.

breakdown.analysis: The councilor takes the residents' rule, applies it, and gets a result that looks absurd: the person who knows the drainage best can't serve. The councilor doesn't like this outcome. It's the absurd result used to sink the rule. The claim supports the conclusion, so it's a premise, but a specific kind: a consequence the councilor rejects.

choices.note: No. The conclusion is the last sentence, about residence being a poor test. The engineer example supports it.
Opposite. The example is aimed against the residents' proposal, not for it.
It's a specific case, not a general principle.

Tempting, because the example does count against the proposal. But it's about the rule giving a bad result, not about enforcement. Nothing suggests the rule would be hard to apply; it applies all too easily.
CORRECT. The councilor derives the engineer's exclusion from the proposed criterion and treats that outcome as unacceptable, which discredits the criterion.

questions.stimulus: Hesketh Railway policy: A train may depart from Corran Station only if its brakes have been inspected that same day. A train's brakes may be inspected only by a crew member who holds a current safety certificate. Any train carrying passengers must also have a conductor aboard, unless it is a shuttle running between Corran and Mill Lane. Today every train complied with this policy, and the 9:15 train, which is carrying passengers and is not a shuttle, departed from Corran Station.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Today a crew member holding a current safety certificate inspected the 9:15 train's brakes.
The conductor aboard the 9:15 train holds a current safety certificate.
Every train that departed from Corran Station today had a conductor aboard.
Any train whose brakes are inspected today by a certified crew member may depart from Corran Station.
No shuttle running between Corran and Mill Lane carried passengers today.
questions.explanation: The 9:15 departed, so its brakes were inspected today, and only certified crew members may inspect brakes, so A must be true. D is the reversal trap: the policy makes an inspection necessary for departure, not sufficient.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Departs Corran → brakes inspected that day; 2. Brakes inspected → by a certified crew member; 3. Carrying passengers AND not a shuttle → conductor aboard; 4. The policy was followed today; 5. The 9:15 carried passengers, isn't a shuttle, and departed Corran.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: 9:15 departed → brakes inspected today → inspector was certified. That's the main chain. Separately, 9:15 had passengers and isn't a shuttle → it had a conductor. Watch for answers that reverse an arrow or apply a rule to trains we know nothing about.

choices.note: CORRECT. Departed → inspected today → inspected by a certified crew member. Both links are in the policy, and the policy was followed.
We don't know this. The 9:15 had a conductor, but nothing says the conductor did the inspection or holds a certificate.
Too broad. Shuttles and trains without passengers don't need conductors, and some of those may have departed today.
This reverses the policy. Inspection is required for departure ('only if'), not a guarantee of it. Other rules could still keep a train in the station.
We don't know. Shuttles are just exempt from the conductor rule; nothing says whether any carried passengers.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Last year the town of Orrin doubled its tax on commercial properties left vacant, in order to push landlords to fill empty storefronts. This year, eleven of the town's thirty empty storefronts have found new tenants. The tax increase, then, has succeeded in reducing the number of empty storefronts in Orrin.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the columnist's argument depends?
choices: Landlords in Orrin generally pay close attention to changes in local tax rates.
The tax increase will continue to reduce the number of empty storefronts in future years.
Not all of the eleven storefronts would have found new tenants this year even if the tax had not been increased.
None of the storefronts in Orrin that were occupied last year has become empty since then.
The doubled tax is higher than the tax on vacant commercial properties in any neighboring town.
questions.explanation: To credit the tax, the columnist must assume that at least some of the new leases would not have happened anyway; negate C (all eleven would have been filled regardless) and the tax accomplished nothing. D is the tempting too-strong trap: a few new vacancies would not sink the argument, so the argument does not need zero.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The tax increase has succeeded in reducing the number of empty storefronts.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the tax doubled, eleven of thirty empty storefronts found tenants.

breakdown.analysis: Eleven storefronts filled. Would they have filled anyway? Storefronts get rented every year. If all eleven would have been leased without the tax, the tax did nothing. A claim that a policy caused something needs the outcome not to have happened anyway. We need an answer that says at least some of those leases depended on the tax.

choices.note: Not required. Negate it: landlords don't generally watch tax rates. Some still could have, and the tax could still have worked.
choices.negation: Landlords in Orrin do not generally pay close attention to tax changes. (A few might, and the argument can survive.)

choices.note: Future years are beside the point. The conclusion is about what the tax has already done.
choices.negation: The tax will not keep reducing vacancies in future years. (Past success is untouched.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: all eleven would have been filled anyway. Then the tax caused none of the drop, and the argument falls apart.
choices.negation: All eleven storefronts would have found tenants this year even without the tax increase.

choices.note: Tempting, because new vacancies could offset the eleven. But 'none' is too strong. Negated, one or two storefronts went empty, and the number of empty storefronts still fell.
choices.negation: At least one storefront that was occupied last year has become empty. (With eleven filled, the total can still drop.)

choices.note: Irrelevant comparison. Orrin's tax could be lower than a neighbor's and still have worked.
choices.negation: Some neighboring town has a tax on vacant properties at least as high as Orrin's. (No effect on whether Orrin's tax worked.)

questions.stimulus: Arts funder: Last season, none of the Kestrel Theater's productions that received a production grant from our foundation lost money. This season, every one of the Kestrel's productions has received such a grant. So none of the Kestrel's productions this season will lose money.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the arts funder's argument?
choices: Last year, every bakery in Dorne that won the city's pastry prize used imported butter. This year the Lark Bakery has switched to imported butter. So the Lark Bakery will win the pastry prize this year.
Last spring, none of the hiking club's members who carried maps got lost. This spring, several members will hike without maps. So several members of the hiking club will get lost this spring.
Every bus on the Route 4 line is inspected monthly, and no bus that is inspected monthly has ever broken down. So no bus on the Route 4 line has ever broken down.

Everyone who failed last year's chemistry final at Hale Academy had skipped the review sessions. This year, every chemistry student at Hale has attended them. So no chemistry student at Hale will fail this year's final.

None of the restaurants on Quay Street that were inspected last month had any health violations. Since those restaurants were chosen at random, probably few restaurants on Quay Street have health violations.
questions.explanation: The funder takes a pattern seen in last season's grant recipients and treats it as guaranteed for a new, larger group; D does the same, phrased in contrapositive form (every failer skipped = no attender failed). A is tempting because it also projects last year onto this year, but it reverses the conditional, inferring the prize from the butter.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: None of the Kestrel's productions this season will lose money.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last season no grant-funded production lost money; this season every production has a grant.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Last time, no X that had Y suffered Z; now all X have Y; so no X will suffer Z.

breakdown.analysis: Why is this bad? Last season's grant winners may have been chosen because they looked like safe bets. Now every production has a grant, including the risky ones. A past pattern among a selected group gets treated as a guarantee for a new, broader group. Find the choice that does the same thing, and don't be thrown by wording: 'everyone who failed had skipped' says exactly the same as 'no one who attended failed.'

choices.note: Tempting, since it projects last year onto this year. But it reverses the conditional: winners had imported butter, so having butter means winning. The stimulus never reverses anything.
Different flaw: denying the antecedent. Map carriers didn't get lost, so non-carriers will. The stimulus applies its pattern to people who have the feature, not to those without it.
This one is valid. If every Route 4 bus is inspected monthly and no such bus has ever broken down, the conclusion follows. The stimulus is flawed; this isn't.
CORRECT. 'Every student who failed had skipped' = 'no one who attended failed.' Now everyone attends, so no one will fail. Same past pattern applied as a guarantee to a new, broader group.
Different reasoning: a random sample used to draw a hedged ('probably few') conclusion about a whole street. That's a reasonable statistical inference, not a past pattern turned into a guarantee.

questions.stimulus: Theater consultant: Companies in the Wells Theater Alliance that took the alliance's grant-writing workshop last year won foundation grants at twice the rate of member companies that did not take it. The alliance should therefore require every member company to take the workshop, since doing so will raise the proportion of its members that win foundation grants.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the theater consultant's argument?
choices: How much the alliance paid the instructor who led last year's grant-writing workshop
Whether foundations prefer to fund theater companies that belong to an alliance
How many of the alliance's member companies applied for foundation grants last year
Whether any of the companies that won foundation grants last year applied to more than one foundation
Whether the companies that took the workshop had already been winning grants at a higher rate beforehand
questions.explanation: Companies chose whether to take the workshop, so the ones that did may already have been the stronger grant writers; E tells us whether the workshop or prior skill explains the gap. B is tempting because it is about what foundations prefer, but every company being compared belongs to the alliance, so the answer cannot affect the comparison.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Requiring every member company to take the workshop will raise the share of members winning grants.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year, companies that took the workshop won grants at twice the rate of those that didn't.

breakdown.analysis: Who signs up for a voluntary grant-writing workshop? Probably the companies already serious about grants. If they were winning more grants before the workshop, the workshop may have added nothing, and forcing everyone to take it won't help. We need a question whose answer separates 'the workshop helped' from 'good grant writers took the workshop.'

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The instructor's fee says nothing about whether the workshop raises the win rate.
Tempting, but every company in the comparison belongs to the alliance. Whatever foundations think of alliances, it can't explain the gap between workshop takers and non-takers.
So? The comparison is already in rates. Knowing the raw count of applicants doesn't tell us whether the workshop caused the difference.
Irrelevant detail. Multiple applications could apply to takers and non-takers alike; it doesn't test whether the workshop made a difference.

CORRECT. If yes, the takers were already better at winning grants and the workshop may deserve no credit. If no, the gap opened after the workshop, which supports the consultant. Either answer matters.

questions.stimulus: Marine ecologist: Some researchers claim that warming water caused the decline of the kelp forests along the Torvik coast. Their main evidence is that the kelp declined most sharply in the years when the water was warmest. But those were also the years in which the population of kelp-eating sea urchins peaked, so the correlation the researchers cite does not show that warming caused the decline. We can therefore conclude that warming water was not a cause of the kelp's decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the marine ecologist's reasoning?
choices: It relies on a mere correlation to conclude that sea urchins caused the kelp's decline.
It treats the failure of the researchers' evidence to establish a claim as if it showed that the claim is false.
It attacks the researchers' motives rather than the evidence they offer.
It fails to consider that the sea-urchin population may have peaked for reasons unrelated to water temperature.
It draws a conclusion about all kelp forests from evidence about a single stretch of coast.
questions.explanation: The ecologist legitimately shows that the researchers' correlation is confounded by the urchin boom, but then leaps to the claim that warming was not a cause at all; B describes that move from 'not shown' to 'false.' A is the tempting trap because the ecologist mentions urchins, but the ecologist never concludes that urchins caused the decline.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Warming water was not a cause of the kelp's decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The researchers' correlation is confounded: the warmest years were also peak urchin years, so the correlation doesn't show warming caused the decline.

breakdown.analysis: The first half of the ecologist's argument is good. The warm years were also urchin years, so the correlation can't prove warming did it. Fine. But then: 'therefore warming was not a cause.' Wait, that's a much bigger claim. Showing that someone's evidence doesn't prove X is not the same as proving X is false. Warming could still have hurt the kelp; we just don't know yet. It's like saying: your alibi witness is unreliable, so you must be guilty. We need an answer that names the jump from 'not proven' to 'disproven.'

choices.note: Tempting, because urchins are the alternative the ecologist raises. But the ecologist only uses urchins to undercut the researchers; the conclusion is about warming, not about urchins causing anything.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Urchins peaked when the kelp declined, so the urchins must have destroyed the kelp.

choices.note: CORRECT. The researchers' evidence fails to show warming caused the decline; the ecologist treats that failure as proof that warming had no role.
Nothing about motives appears. The ecologist addresses the researchers' evidence directly.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Those researchers are funded by climate groups, so their claim about warming can be dismissed.

choices.note: So? If urchins peaked for unrelated reasons, the confound is even cleaner. This wouldn't hurt the ecologist's point that the correlation is unreliable; it isn't where the argument goes wrong.
choices.example: Example of a real failure to consider: Urchins peaked in warm years, so the kelp loss was due to urchins (ignoring that warmth may have caused the urchin boom).

choices.note: The conclusion is about the Torvik coast only. No generalization to all kelp forests.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Kelp on the Torvik coast wasn't hurt by warming, so warming doesn't harm kelp anywhere.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The Halden Prize committee may consider a play only if that play premiered within the two years before the committee meets. Marrow Lane was first performed three years ago, in a workshop staging before a small invited audience; its first full professional production opened only last spring. Therefore, the committee may not consider Marrow Lane.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the critic's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: A play premieres no later than the first time it is performed before an audience.
Any play that premiered within the two years before the committee meets may be considered by the committee.
A play need not have had a full professional production in order to be considered by the committee.
The committee may not consider any play that has been performed only in workshop stagings.
Theater critics typically count a workshop staging before an invited audience as a play's premiere.
questions.explanation: The rule makes a premiere within two years necessary, so the critic needs Marrow Lane's premiere to fall outside that window; A guarantees it, since the play was first performed three years ago and so premiered then or earlier. D is the most attractive trap, but it covers only plays performed solely in workshops, and Marrow Lane also had a full production; B merely reverses the rule.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The committee may not consider Marrow Lane.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Considered → premiered within the last two years; Marrow Lane was first performed (in a workshop) three years ago; its first full production opened last spring.

breakdown.analysis: When did Marrow Lane premiere: at the workshop three years ago, or at the full production last spring? The argument never says. Chain: Considered → premiered within 2 years. Contrapositive: NOT premiered within 2 years → NOT considered. So we need: Marrow Lane did NOT premiere within 2 years. The only way to get there is to tie 'premiere' to the first performance. If a play premieres no later than its first performance, Marrow Lane premiered three or more years ago → not within 2 years → not considered. Notice that the rule is a necessary condition; an answer that turns it into a sufficient one won't help.

choices.note: CORRECT. First performance was three years ago, so the premiere was then or earlier: outside the two-year window. Contrapositive of the rule: not considered. The conclusion is locked in. The awkward wording is typical of right answers.
This reverses the rule. It tells us which plays may be considered, which can only help a play get in. It can't establish that Marrow Lane is excluded.
Tempting, because it hints the full production doesn't matter. But it doesn't say when Marrow Lane premiered, so we still can't tell whether it falls outside the window.
Tempting, because it targets workshops. But Marrow Lane had a full professional production too, so it wasn't performed 'only' in workshops. The rule doesn't reach it.
Critics' habits aren't the committee's rule. 'Typically' also leaves room for exceptions. This makes the conclusion more plausible but doesn't guarantee it.

questions.stimulus: Rail engineer: On the Calder line, broken rails are reported far more often in winter than in summer. Some attribute this to the heavier freight traffic that the line carries in winter. But the more likely cause is that cold makes the steel rails contract, putting them under tension that can open small flaws into breaks.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the rail engineer's argument?
choices: Freight traffic on the Calder line is heavier in winter than in any other season.
Steel rails also expand in hot weather, which can cause them to buckle.
Most of the Calder line's rails were installed more than thirty years ago.
Most winter rail breaks on the line occur just before dawn, when it is coldest and freight traffic is lightest.
Winter rail breaks on the Calder line are most common on the stretches that carry the most freight.
questions.explanation: If breaks cluster in the coldest hours, when freight traffic is at its lightest, the timing fits the contraction mechanism and cuts against the traffic explanation, so D strengthens. B is the on-topic trap: it adds another effect of temperature on rails, but buckling in summer heat says nothing about why rails break in winter.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Winter rail breaks on the Calder line are more likely caused by cold contraction than by heavier freight traffic.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Breaks are far more common in winter; cold makes steel contract and puts rails under tension.

breakdown.analysis: Two suspects: cold and freight. Both are higher in winter, so seasonal data alone can't separate them. What could? Finer timing. If the mechanism is cold contraction, breaks should pile up when it's coldest. If it's freight, they should pile up when trains are heaviest. We need an answer that pulls those apart in the cold's favor.

choices.note: This supports the rival explanation. Heavier winter freight is exactly what the other side relies on. Wrong direction.
Tempting, since it shows temperature matters for rails. But it's about heat and buckling, not cold and breaks. It doesn't help decide between cold and freight in winter.
Irrelevant. Old rails could break from either cause; this doesn't favor one.
CORRECT. Breaks cluster when it's coldest and freight is lightest. The timing matches the contraction mechanism and points away from traffic.
This points to freight. Breaks tracking freight volume weakens the engineer's claim.

questions.stimulus: Every taxpayer in the province of Velm recently answered a survey about provincial taxes. Most of them said that they believe they pay a larger share of their income in provincial taxes than most other Velm taxpayers do. Many also said that provincial taxes are too high.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following is most strongly supported by them?
choices: Most taxpayers in Velm are mistaken about how the share of their income that they pay in provincial taxes compares with that of other Velm taxpayers.
Velm's provincial taxes place a heavier burden on most taxpayers than those taxpayers believe.
Some taxpayers in Velm overestimate how the share of their income that they pay in provincial taxes compares with the shares paid by other Velm taxpayers.
Most taxpayers in Velm pay a smaller share of their income in provincial taxes than they believe they pay.
The Velm taxpayers who pay the largest share of their income in provincial taxes are the most likely to say that provincial taxes are too high.
questions.explanation: It is impossible for most taxpayers to pay a larger share than most others, so some of those who believe they do must be wrong, and wrong in the direction of overrating their own share relative to others; that is C. A is the tempting trap: if, say, 60 percent hold the belief and about half really are above the middle, only around 10 percent need be mistaken, far short of most.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Every Velm taxpayer answered; 2. most believe they pay a larger share of income in provincial taxes than most other Velm taxpayers; 3. many think taxes are too high.

breakdown.analysis: Can most people really pay more than most others? No. To pay more than most others, you have to be above the middle, and at most about half the people can be above the middle. So if more than half believe they're above the middle, some of them must be wrong. But only some. Imagine 100 taxpayers: 60 believe they're in the top half, and the top half really holds 50. At least 10 are wrong. Ten is not most. Watch the subset trap: 'some are mistaken' follows; 'most are mistaken' doesn't.

choices.note: Tempting, and it's the classic trap. The numbers force only some mistakes, not most. With 60 believers and 50 real top-halfers, as few as 10 need be wrong.
Wrong direction and unsupported. If anything, the mistaken ones think their burden is relatively larger than it is.
CORRECT. More than half can't all be above the middle, so some who think they pay a larger share than most others don't. They overrate their relative position.
Wrong dimension. The belief is about rank compared with others, not about the size of one's own share. Someone could know their own share exactly and simply underestimate everyone else's.
We don't know this. The stimulus never links actual tax share to opinions about whether taxes are too high.

questions.stimulus: Election commissioner: A candidate for the Bramford town council should be exempted from the requirement to collect petition signatures if the candidate either currently holds an elected town office or has been nominated by a party that received at least 10 percent of the vote in the most recent council election, provided that the candidate has also filed a financial disclosure statement by the filing deadline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated by the election commissioner?
choices: Okafor, who was nominated by a party that received 12 percent of the vote in the most recent council election, should be exempted, since that party's nominees have been exempted in the past.
Lindqvist, who holds no elected office and who filed her financial disclosure on time, should not be exempted, since she has not been nominated by any party.
Varga, who filed his financial disclosure on time and who served on the town council until last year, should be exempted.
Haddad, who currently serves as town clerk, an elected town office, should be exempted, since she plans to file her financial disclosure next week.
Brandt, who was nominated by a party that received 15 percent of the vote in the most recent council election and who filed his financial disclosure two days before the deadline, should be exempted.
questions.explanation: An exemption is warranted when the candidate meets either the office or the party condition and has also filed disclosure by the deadline; Brandt meets the party condition and filed early, so E conforms. B is tempting, but the principle states only when a candidate should be exempted, not when one should be refused, so it cannot justify denying Lindqvist an exemption.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: (Currently holds elected town office OR nominated by a party with 10%+ in the last council election) AND disclosure filed by deadline → should be exempted from petition signatures.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the candidate who should be exempted and who meets every condition.

breakdown.analysis: The right answer must check three things: 1. a positive judgment (exempt), since the rule only says when to exempt; 2. either current elected office or a 10-percent party nomination; 3. disclosure filed by the deadline. Each trap leaves one of these unknown or unmet.

choices.note: The party condition is met, but we don't know whether Okafor filed the disclosure. Past practice isn't one of the conditions.

Tempting, because Lindqvist does fail both the office and party conditions. But the rule tells you only when to exempt someone. It's silent about when to refuse, so it can't back a 'should not' judgment.
Fails the office condition. Varga served until last year; the rule requires currently holding office. And no party nomination is mentioned.
The office condition is met, but disclosure is only planned for next week, and we don't know if that's before the deadline. Condition 3 is unknown.
CORRECT. Party with 15 percent (meets the 10 percent condition), disclosure filed before the deadline, and a positive judgment. Every condition is satisfied.

questions.stimulus: Psychologist: In a study of people beginning a twelve-week course of therapy, clients who were told at the outset that therapy often feels worse before it feels better were twice as likely to complete the full course as clients who were not told this. Yet among the clients who completed the course, those who had been told reported no greater improvement than those who had not. So telling clients what to expect does nothing to increase the number of clients who improve.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the psychologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that clients who complete a course of therapy improve more than clients who do not complete it
treats a correlation between being told what to expect and completing therapy as proof that being told causes clients to complete it
fails to establish that the clients who were told what to expect understood what they were told
ignores the possibility that telling clients what to expect increases the number who improve by increasing the number who complete therapy
confuses the claim that being told what to expect is not sufficient for improvement with the claim that it is not necessary for improvement
questions.explanation: The study shows that telling clients doubles completion and leaves improvement among completers unchanged; if completing therapy helps, telling clients would raise the total number who improve simply by getting more of them to the end, which is the possibility D says the argument ignores. A is the strongest trap because it names the key factor, but the argument does not assume that completers improve more; if anything, it needs the opposite.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Telling clients what to expect does nothing to increase the number of clients who improve.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Told clients were twice as likely to finish; among finishers, told and untold clients improved equally.

breakdown.analysis: Improvement per finisher was the same. Does that mean the number who improve is the same? No. Telling clients doubled the number who finished. If finishing therapy helps, then twice as many finishers means more improved people overall, even though each finisher improves the same amount. The psychologist compares people inside the finisher group and forgets that the size of that group changed. It's like saying a free-shuttle program doesn't increase concert attendance at the arena because each rider enjoys the show the same as people who drove; the point is that more people got there. We need an answer that says more completions can mean more improvement in total.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about the exact factor that matters. But it's backwards. The argument doesn't assume finishers improve more; if they do, the argument fails. The flaw is ignoring that possibility, not assuming it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Clients who finished improved, so finishing therapy must be what made them improve more than dropouts.

choices.note: The argument doesn't rely on this causal claim. Accepting that being told causes completion would actually work against its conclusion.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Told clients finished more often, so being told must be what made them finish.

choices.note: So? Whether they understood or not, the study measured the outcomes. This doesn't touch the gap between per-finisher improvement and total improvement.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Clients told about side effects had fewer complaints, so the warning worked (without checking they understood it).

choices.note: CORRECT. Same improvement per finisher, but twice as many finishers. If finishing helps, total improvement rises. The argument looks only inside the finisher group and ignores the change in its size.
No conditional confusion. The argument never talks about what is necessary or sufficient for improvement.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Being told what to expect doesn't guarantee improvement, so clients can improve without being told.

questions.stimulus: Museum conservator: Since our museum switched to a new lighting system in its galleries, the number of paintings found to have new damage at our annual inspection has fallen from about twenty a year to about twelve. So the new lighting system has made our galleries a less harmful environment for paintings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conservator's argument?
choices: Most damage found since the switch has been deep cracking needing extensive repair; most found before was slight fading.
The new lighting system uses considerably less electricity than the system it replaced.
Some of the paintings found damaged before the switch had been harmed by careless handling rather than by light.
Visitors report that paintings are easier to see under the new lighting system than under the old one.
The annual inspections both before and after the switch were carried out by the same team of conservators.
questions.explanation: The conservator measures harm by counting damaged paintings, but fewer cases of far more serious damage could mean the galleries are now more harmful, which is what A shows. C is tempting because it suggests not all damage came from light, but it says nothing about any change after the switch, so it does not explain the drop away.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new lighting has made the galleries less harmful for paintings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Paintings found with new damage fell from about twenty a year to about twelve after the switch.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of damaged paintings really the measure of harm? Twelve paintings with deep cracks can be far worse than twenty with a little fading. The conservator counts cases but ignores severity. That's a measure mismatch. We need an answer that shows the damage got worse even as the count went down.

choices.note: CORRECT. Fewer cases, but much more serious ones. Deep cracking needing extensive repair versus slight fading means total harm may have gone up. The count no longer shows a less harmful environment.
Wrong dimension. Electricity use is about cost, not about harm to paintings.
Tempting, since it suggests light wasn't the only cause of damage. But nothing says handling changed after the switch. Without that, it doesn't explain the drop. Merely possible isn't enough.
Irrelevant. How well visitors can see the paintings says nothing about harm to them.
This strengthens the argument by ruling out a change in inspectors as the reason for the drop. Wrong direction.

questions.stimulus: Railway official: Our rule against bringing bicycles onto rush-hour trains exists only to keep the aisles clear for passengers. A folding bicycle, once folded, takes up no more room than a briefcase. So the rule should not be applied to passengers carrying folded bicycles.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the railway official's argument?
choices: The pool forbids glass containers because broken glass is hard to see in water. Plastic containers cannot shatter. So the pool should require that all drinks be served in plastic containers.
Holt Park's campfire ban exists solely to prevent wildfires. Gas stoves with enclosed flames pose no risk of starting a wildfire. So the ban should not be enforced against people using such stoves.
The rule that hikers register before climbing Mount Feld is intended to help rescuers find lost hikers. Rescuers have rarely needed the register. So the rule should be abolished.
The museum forbids flash photography because camera flashes can fade old pigments. Many visitors ignore the rule. So the museum should enforce it more strictly.

Our firm forbids personal phone calls during meetings because they distract other attendees. A brief call is less distracting than a long one. So brief calls should be penalized less severely than long ones.
questions.explanation: The official reasons that a rule's sole purpose does not apply to a certain case, so the rule should not be applied to that case; B has the same structure with the campfire ban and enclosed stoves. C is tempting because it also reasons from a rule's purpose, but it concludes that the whole rule should be abolished, not that one kind of case should be exempt.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bicycle rule should not be applied to folded bicycles.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The rule's only purpose is keeping aisles clear; folded bikes don't block aisles.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Rule R exists only to prevent harm H; case C doesn't produce H; so R shouldn't be applied to C.

breakdown.analysis: Three parts to match: 1. a rule with a single stated purpose; 2. a kind of case that doesn't threaten that purpose; 3. the conclusion that the rule shouldn't apply to that kind of case (an exemption, not a new rule, not repeal). Check the conclusion of each choice first; that kills most of them fast.

choices.note: The conclusion is a new requirement (all drinks in plastic), not an exemption from the existing rule.
CORRECT. Sole purpose: prevent wildfires. Enclosed stoves don't risk wildfires. So don't enforce the ban against them. Exact match.
Tempting, because it reasons from the rule's purpose. But the conclusion is to abolish the rule for everyone, based on how rarely it's needed. The official exempts one kind of case.
Different direction: people break the rule, so enforce it harder. No case is shown to fall outside the rule's purpose.
The conclusion is about grading penalties, not about exempting a case. Brief calls still distract, just less.

questions.stimulus: Fisheries officer: Lionfish, an invasive predator on the Calder Reef, eat large numbers of young reef fish. Last year we began paying divers a bounty for each lionfish they spear on the reef. Since then, divers have killed thousands of lionfish there, so the bounty program must be easing the pressure on the reef's young fish.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the fisheries officer's argument requires which one of the following assumptions?
choices: Lionfish are the most important predator of young fish on the Calder Reef.
Divers collecting the bounty do not spear any fish other than lionfish while on the reef.
The lionfish killed by divers have not been fully replaced by new lionfish arriving on the reef or hatching there.
The bounty program will eventually eliminate every lionfish from the Calder Reef.
Most of the lionfish killed by divers were adults rather than juveniles.
questions.explanation: Killing thousands of lionfish helps young reef fish only if the lionfish population actually ends up smaller, so the argument requires C. Negate C (the dead fish were fully replaced) and predation is unchanged. A and D are too strong: lionfish need not be the top predator, and the program need not wipe them out, for the pressure to ease.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bounty program must be easing predation pressure on the reef's young fish.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lionfish eat many young reef fish; divers have killed thousands of lionfish since the bounty began.

breakdown.analysis: Thousands killed. So what if thousands more showed up? Invasive species often bounce back fast. If new lionfish moved in or hatched as quickly as divers removed them, the reef has as many lionfish as before, and the young fish are no better off. We need an answer that says the kills weren't fully offset.

choices.note: Too strong. Lionfish can be the second-biggest predator and removing them still eases pressure.
choices.negation: Lionfish are not the most important predator of young fish on the reef. (Removing them can still help.)

choices.note: Too strong. A diver spearing the occasional grouper doesn't undo the benefit of thousands of dead lionfish.
choices.negation: Some divers spear at least one other kind of fish. (Pressure from lionfish can still be eased.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the dead lionfish were replaced one for one or more. Then the reef holds just as many predators, and the pressure hasn't eased. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: The lionfish killed have been replaced by an equal or greater number of new lionfish.

choices.note: Too strong, and about the future. Easing pressure doesn't require total elimination.
choices.negation: The program will not eliminate lionfish from the reef. (Fewer lionfish can still mean less pressure.)

choices.note: Tempting, since big adults eat more. But juveniles eat young fish too, and killing them prevents future predators. Negated, the argument survives.
choices.negation: Most of the lionfish killed were juveniles. (Killing them still removes predators.)
